utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like first to welcome everyone in this courtroom, Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, our witness, as well as the interpreters and all our technical staff. Before giving the floor to Mr. Seselj, who would like to take the floor regarding two topics, two housekeeping matters, I would like to say that later, once the Dragomir Milosevic judgement is rendered, we will move to Courtroom I. And we can also work until 2.45 p.m. Yesterday we were a bit late. We were an hour late. I hope the Prosecution will speed up, and that way Mr. Seselj would carry out his cross-examination as planned. I would also like to tell Mrs. Dahl that you told Chamber -- the Trial Chamber that you wanted to tender a number of documents regarding the various speeches and interventions of Mr. Seselj, the list of which is in a summary chart. The rule here is as such: A document can be tendered and admitted when a -- when a witness has recognized the document. This is the general principle. And the case -- this also is confirmed by the case law of the appeals and -- allow to admit a number of exhibits that have not been shown to a witness. If these -- and this will apply in the case here because these are speeches of Mr. Seselj. But there needs to be a written submission. And Defence, i.e., Mr. Seselj, must be able to comment on this. And then the Trial Chamber will render a written decision. Mrs. Dahl, I hope you see -- this is what I had to say. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, before we turn to Mr. Seselj's housekeeping matters, I'd like to be recognized so I respond to what you just said. I have two brief points. First, I acknowledge your request that the Prosecution speed up. The inference that people may draw from that is that there is some fault to be attributed to the Prosecution for the use of time yesterday. I wish to indicate that if there is any reason for the length of time yesterday went, it has to do with housekeeping and lengthy speaking objections by Mr. Seselj. I do not wish to get to the end of the case and find that things have proceeded longer than expected and then to have some adverse inference drawn against the Prosecution in the presentation of our case. We are proceeding with all deliberate speed and efficiently using our time. With regard to the documents uttered by Mr. Seselj, I provided him a list of what we wanted to admit to see whether he had objections. I understand you're requesting a written motion through which to tender those documents. I will prepare that for you. I will not have it, of course, tomorrow morning, when I had intended to offer the documents in for admission. I also wish to state that I disagree with your explication of the law on how documents are admitted. I understand that bringing them in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, I'll just stop you here. Whether you agree with me or not, this is not my problem. If you're not -- if you don't agree with me, you can ask for a certification of appeal. You can sit down. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I first have to deal with these two issues very briefly and then the next three, very briefly. Mrs. Dahl, as the Prosecutor, does not have the right to object about my yesterday's objections, because they were all justified. She would be entitled to complain if I had made unjustified objections just to take up time. Since all my objections were justified, she has no right to complain whatsoever. Second, I received a list of those exhibits from the Prosecution that are tendered, but I received only part of the exhibits yesterday. The Prosecution said I would receive the rest today. Most of those documents are such that I would have no objection to them being admitted; however, there are some documents to which I would not agree, and I will state my reasons tomorrow, because the Prosecution said they will be discussed tomorrow. Today I'm not prepared. Those were those two things. I have already said to the representative of the Registry my two objections, but I have three. The third did not have to do with the Registry. First of all, the public nature of this trial is jeopardized because there was no broadcast yesterday on the Internet. Every time I appear in the courtroom, there's always some problem with the Internet. I made two submissions indicating the falsifying of transcript, the intentional falsifying of the transcript, and the extremely bad interpretation. Now my associates cannot follow the Internet broadcast and it is a big question how I will be able to find errors in the transcript in the future. I know that the world public is very interest -- has a great interest in this trial. Second, concerning the trial. I asked the Registry that in the break between two sessions I should be able to use the telephone in my room, like Mr. Milosevic did. They had promised me that, but now I don't have that possibility, so they broke their promise. Now, in the breaks, I need to call my associates, who might be able to hear the Internet broadcast, to hear their proposal, new information, suggestions, et cetera. This way I am isolated, lonely here. Between two sessions I have no opportunity to do anything, and I need to. And third, yesterday I received from the Prosecution, with confirmation 139, some documents about Mr. Oberschall exclusively in English. It's absolutely useless to me. I have no translations in Serbian. In the opening statement, the Prosecutor said that they provided these documents as a response to the decision of the Trial Chamber. I never heard of such a thing. How can one respond to the decision of the Trial Chamber? I heard of appeals being made, given a certification, but to reply to a decision of the Trial Chamber, I never heard of that before. This was probably made available to you in French and in English. It was given me in English. It is useless to me, and I cannot state my opinion. There are 10 to 15 pages here -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'll be very quick. Regarding the Internet first. You are right. I have checked lately, and it -- whether it worked, and it -- I was told it did not work. I asked why, and I still haven't been given the reasons. So just like you, I'm starting to wonder whether somebody isn't doing this on purpose to block your Internet transmission, because this is quite unacceptable. Supposedly for a technical problem that's been going on for weeks, we have no Internet broadcast and there are no solutions. Regarding the phone now. Mr. Registrar will do what is necessary, since Mr. Milosevic could talk to his associates, you should be allowed to do this too. Now, thirdly, regarding the documents that you obtained in English, you were supposed to get them in your own language, of course. We handed down a decision on November 30th, 2007. And for very obscure reasons this decision was not translated. It seems that the translation department made a mistake as to the deadline for translation. And we asked Prosecution to identify the questions and to disclose to Trial Chamber and to yourself all required documents. So you have -- this is why you have them, but I guess they didn't have time to translate them in your language. So now you have the reason. I'm sure that Mrs. Dahl has something to add to confirm this. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: First I want to respond to Mr. Seselj's statement that we did not provide him with the exhibits that we intend to tender tomorrow. That is simply not true. We gave him a list of the subset of the exhibit list. All of the exhibits have been disclosed to him already. As a courtesy, we are reprinting exhibit binders. That is a tremendous production load. And rather than taking the information we gave to Mr. Seselj regarding the exhibit list in the format that we could produce it, he rejected it. So he is depriving himself of the information that is available to him. There is a significant problem that needs to be resolved. We will start first with the Registrar. Mr. Seselj needs additional facilities for his self-representation in the form of a qualified language assistant. We, the Prosecution, work in the official languages of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, we're not going to deal with this problem. The Trial Chamber knows it inside out. We did note that the Prosecution was supposed to give all documents to the accused in his own language. Don't talk about a language assistant. He's supposed to get the documents in his own language. If he does not get them --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That is not what I understood the order to say. You asked me to give him essentially an outline of my direct examination, which is unheard of in this Tribunal that the Prosecution has to give the accused a list of the questions he's going to ask. I thought it would help move the examination along. I did not see any reason to quarrel with the order, and I did it to the best of my ability. I cannot prepare for trial and absorb the burden of translating for Mr. Seselj material to work in court. That is not the Prosecution's obligation, to translate, to serve as his trial assistant, to translate, to enable him to work in the official languages of this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, when you have documents, you must send them to the translation department and the translation department will then send the documents to him once translated. I'm not asking you to translate them. If you can't translate them yourself, give them to the translation department. But Mr. Seselj must be given the documents in his own language. Notably if it is a document that you're going to use when the witness is here. If the document is not translated, you will have a problem. So later on, if you have exhibits that need to be disclosed to Mr. Seselj - and they might be after some kind of proofing - give them to the translation unit and the translation unit will send them to Mr. Seselj once translated. Then you're talking about tomorrow. Both of you are talking about tomorrow. But I had understood that yesterday was your day; today was Mr. Seselj's day; and tomorrow there was supposed to be another witness, and he's not going to be there. So why are you talking about tomorrow? Normally everything is supposed to done by tonight -- by today.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This concerns the exhibits that were authored or uttered by Mr. Seselj. That's what is intended for tomorrow. I think before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is on -- what's going on tomorrow? What's going on tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Tomorrow I had intended to publish the exhibits that Mr. Seselj has no objection to entering into evidence and to move those over his objection that the Court finds relevant and probative. What you've told me this morning, though, is that you would like an additional written motion so that you can take that under advisement. I wanted to make sure, though, that we hear from the translation department about their ability to comply with what your direction is, because I think that it places an unreasonable burden on them and that the burden belongs to Mr. Seselj, consequent upon his decision to represent himself, and that the Registrar should give him a language assistant to help him make access to documents in the official language of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So regarding tomorrow, it -- tomorrow you wanted to do the necessary regarding these documents. But normally tomorrow there will be no hearing, unless you can find a new witness, because we will finish with this witness today. It's already 9.20. We must absolutely move on. And you have the floor for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say and to add. I would like to ask the witness [as interpreted] to not get into useless controversies. Notably, when he was saying that Mrs. Dahl raised an objection against his own objections. Mr. Seselj, I really have not understood that in the -- in a similar way, just explained -- she was just explaining why her in-chief was longer than expected yesterday. That's all. I mean, in the interest of justice and in your own interest, you should -- we have to be able to make headway without useless controversies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I absolutely agree with my fellow Judge. There should be no controversy in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I have to respond to that. It seems that the interpretation you are getting is really a disaster. I was saying here something about the document of the Prosecution, which says that this is the response to the decision of the Trial Chamber regarding the status of Witness Oberschall. I never heard that a response may be made to a decision of the Trial Chamber. That's the gist of what I said. As for my yesterday's objections, I only said that they were all justified and that I did not waste time. And third, this list of exhibits, the Prosecution first gave it to me in English, so I wrote a letter to Mrs. Dahl and requested them in English [as interpreted]. Last Monday I got them in Serbian. Yesterday I received the first box of documents. Mrs. Dahl says that it is a matter of courtesy on the part of the Prosecution that documents are delivered again, served again, just before they are used. It's not a courtesy. It is an obligation that you imposed on the Prosecution that before a witness is heard, the documents have to be provided again. Why would I otherwise take a list of 15, 20 pages and then look all across my archive to find these documents? It would take me two or three days. It's normal that they serve them again. It's done in every other trial. Binders are made just before a witness appears and submitted to all parties. It was not avoided in any other trial. It's not a courtesy. It's an obligation. Of course I had received those documents before. But just before they are used, the Prosecution has to select them and make them available to me. It's done everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I misspoke. You did order us to do it. However, it is the exception in the trials in this Tribunal. It is only this case and the other case that you preside over where people -- the Prosecution is required to create paper witness binders. Every single document that we will bring up in court is available in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that's the way it is. And you have to comply with this. Now, please continue with your in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Oberschall. I'd like to return to the discussion of the examples you coded concerning Mr. Seselj's call for the expulsion of civilians during the war. May I ask you, please, to turn to example number 100. That is Marked for Identification Exhibit P3. The English e-court number is at page 152, and the B/C/S page number is at 138. This is the record that begins: "In this village, too, in Hrtkovci, in this place in Serb Srem, there is no room for Croats." Have you found that record?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Reviewing the record, could you identify how you coded the record.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I coded it as "expulsion/exchange of population" and also "victimhood."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you indicate what part of the text you found to constitute a call for expulsion or exchange of population.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very first sentence reads: "There is no room for Croats." Then four lines down: "All the rest must clear out of Serbia." And: "We will drive them to the border of Serb territory and they can walk on from there if they do not leave before on their own accord."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is the date of the utterance of this speech?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's May 6, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn the page to example number 101.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you find in this record additional examples of calls for expulsion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You will promptly get rid of the remaining Croats in your and surrounding villages." I think that's pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is that from the same speech that we just heard an excerpt of?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, May 6, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you now to go to example 141, which is at e-court page 212; in B/C/S it's at page 189. This is from a radio broadcast in October 26, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you identify what portion of the text you coded as "expulsion and exchange of population."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the very first sentence says: "We insist that a civilised exchange of the population be carried out with Croatia," and goes into two reasons. One, that Tudjman expelled 300.000 Serbs and the other one, because in World War II, 500.000 Serbs -- I'm sorry, Ante Pavelic settled some of the worst, he says, Ustasha from Western Herzegovina in towns in Vojvodina, and he gives examples of particular -- particular groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Which towns was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slankamen, Hrtkovci, Petrovaradin, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Seselj say should happen there? Or what is he -- I'm sorry, let me rephrase that. What is he explaining about what he had previously advocated in those towns?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says: "We advocated an exchange of population there; namely, that the Croats return to their original homes" - I suppose he means where they lived before World War II or during -- or up to World War II - "and that the Serbs who had already been expelled by Tudjman move into their apartments, that they exchange homes and apartments, and that process has been completed, in my view." So he's talking about something that has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you -- I want to turn now to the effect of propaganda as a tool of mass persuasion.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We touched briefly on this yesterday. How does -- can you briefly summarise, how does propaganda work?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, propaganda works by -- propaganda is a technique of persuasion that is based on emotional appeals and on basically a -- a sense of -- creating a sense of threat against -- against people, who then become anxious and filled with fear, and who then demand that this threat be removed. And, of course, political leaders come and say that, We are here to protect you and to remove that threat. Give us your vote, enlist in our armed forces, and we will do it for you. So through negative stereotyping, through generalisations, appeals to victimhood, creating a sense of threat, the -- on -- on the positive side, you create a demand for action, including violent action; and on the negative side, if you deprive the adversaries and the opponents of access to the media, basically they do not get access to two sides of an -- of an argument and of the reasons for undertaking certain actions. And if you repeat this often enough in the context of this threatening situation, they will be persuaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Is the audience an important component of propaganda discourse?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, what we've been talking about, there's a -- in discourse, there's a messenger, there's a message, and there's the audience that is supposed to be persuaded. Now, the messenger in this case we're discussing is Dr. Seselj. The message is what I have content analysed, and we've been, you know, discussing details of it as to how I went about doing it and what he said in various settings. Now, all of that is not for the amusement of anybody; it's to persuade them in a political sense to give them -- to -- the audience will vote for him, vote for his political party or people who are the leaders of the political points of view that he represents. And that is, sort of, say, the final chapter in this drama is how the audience reacts to all this propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let me turn to some video-clips now. You mentioned access to the media. What's the importance of re-broadcasting by newscasters or the media of speeches by political person -- persons speaking in -- about political issues of the day?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I didn't quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What's the importance of access to the media and the re-broadcast of speeches by a politician?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have shown material here based on research done by Serb political scientists during this time that the Milosevic and affiliated nationalist political parties and leaders, like Dr. Seselj, except for a brief period of time when he and Milosevic didn't agree, they had about 90 per cent of the television audience and not quite as much, in terms of the total audience, for -- for political messages, were really in the hands of -- of, I would say, the -- Milosevic and other nationalist groups, like Dr. Seselj and his -- and his Radical Party, which is enormous. I mean, it's not quite what the Soviet Union had under Stalin, and so on, which is much closer to 100 per cent. But 90 per cent is a -- is a big number. And especially since this number was really close to 100 per cent when it comes to the population of Serbia living outside of the capital, Belgrade, where there was a more limited pluralist opportunity for the opposition to voice their views.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to a news programme by Serbian television Studio B, that is dated November 6, 1991. This is 65 ter number 6034. And it's a report on volunteers signing up at the Radical Party office, followed by a speech given by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] For the final liberation of Vukovar. In response to the question whether volunteers would be sent to Grubisno Polje, one of the volunteers said that Vukovar was a priority and only later the other areas. This is what Branko Vasiljevic told us. How old are you? 58. Where are you from? Nis. Where have you set out? I have set out to help my brothers. Are you alone? No. I have two sons. Are they here as well? They came 10 or 15 days ago. One is in Borovo and one in Knin. Blood runs thicker than water. Mr. Seselj made a speech in front of the group of volunteers and said: "God bless you, heroes, volunteers. God bless you too. Brother Serbs, Serb Chetnik heroes, you are going to the new war today. Today you are going to liberate Serb Vukovar and defend Serb Slavonia. You are going to join hundreds and thousands of our volunteers. You are leaving from all parts of today's reduced Serbia to restore the glory of Serbian arms and the Serbian army. You are going to cooperate with the Yugoslav army because it is our army. It is, first of all, our army in terms of the officer cadre and its fight for Serb territories. Mr. Seselj finished with the following words: "Good luck, guys. See you in Vukovar." These words of Seselj's mean that he, too, will join the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party remains to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Dr. Oberschall, can you describe the effect of Dr. Seselj's discourse on his audience -- oh, first can -- did -- in the course of studying his materials, did you identify his targeted audience?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought these were volunteers that his party -- that he and his party organised, I think in Belgrade, for the purpose of, you know, training them and sending them to the Vukovar front, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In looking for the effect of propaganda on the audience, how important is it -- or first, is it important to identify speech patterns or repetition of ideas articulated by the audience?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, what you see in this -- in this video is a very close relationship that he has to the volunteers. They listen to him. They repeat some of the reasons and phrases that he uses. And you can also see him as a -- in a -- in a leadership position. I mean, he's the important person who has organised and motivated these volunteers. They listen to him and they -- and they follow his guidance. And it's -- you can see how he stands there talking to the volunteers as they go off to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Okay. Let me now turn to another video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to have a number for this video-clip we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry. I'd like to move that video-clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P17.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This next clip is 6058 on our 65 ter exhibit number, and it is two clips. One is -- this is dated May 13, 1993, produced by Srpska Radio Television. And it's a report on the Serbian Radical Party leadership visiting Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] There are no borders among Serbs, as was said. There are no frontiers, as was said in Banja Luka. The Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina are the pride of all Serbdom. The Serbian people west of Drina is a victor in the battlefield and cannot lose the battle at the green negotiating table, as their enemies and foreign agents would desire. The Drina will never be a border, since the Drina is a river running through the centre of Serbia, said Vojvoda Seselj. Drina will never be the border. Drina is a river running through the centre of Serbia. Muslims and Croats do not represent a threat to us for a long time already. Only brothers and sisters Serbs, there should be no hesitating, waiting, or truce. The next time they strike, we should finish them off so they never strike back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And let me follow that with clip B from the same -- this is a -- I'm sorry, before we do that --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's pause that, please. Let me move that one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit -- Your Honours, Exhibit number P18.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. The date of this rally should be referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the date? Mr. Seselj must know, but for the record, what is the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'll repeat the date. It is May 13, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What aspects of propaganda, Dr. Oberschall, did you hear in that discourse?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a -- actually, a very good example of the threat removal; that is to say, he says, We've been threatened. We might be threatened again. And I guarantee you we will remove the threat. That was the -- in the speech that he gave from the podium, was pretty standard threat and threat removal kinds of -- kinds of discourse.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me show you another speech. This one is from April 14, 1992. It is clip B from 65 ter number 6058.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] We, the Serbian radicals, swear once again here before you that we will not allow the Drina to be the border, that Drina will be the river running through the centre of Serbia. Brothers and sisters Serbs, with joint forces, with our harmony and unity, we will unite the Serbian territories and create a Greater Serbia. And now, Serbian brothers and sisters, let's go peacefully and proudly to the Serbian Drina, to the Sepacki Bridge. And at the end we have to say the people were today honoured to be protected at the Drina Bridge by strong police forces. Truly a real people's police.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What aspects of propaganda can we see in this speech?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I say, first of all, that in the previous clip and in this clip you see the extraordinary influence and popularity that Dr. Seselj has. He's got thousands of people who come out to hear him. They cheer him. He's the centre of -- of attention. They listen to him. And I must say I'm a bit envious. I used to lecture to 40 and 50 students, and here he is, you know, with thousands listening and cheering to him, which never happened to me. But then I was not a politician. But in any case, on the -- on the substantive end, it's -- the second clipping shows, first of all, his view of Greater Serbia and basically arbitrary removal of -- of -- of international borders as a way of achieving this, because after all, the Drina is an international border at this particular time. And the second thing is the intimate relationship between advocacy and action, because he not only talks about removing the Drina border but symbolically he and thousands of others walk down to the river and the -- and -- and the bridge and they actually cross this border and sort of symbolically say it doesn't really exist. We're all part of the same Greater Serbia. So it's a very impressive kind of event, in terms of visual image and propaganda and rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Based on your study of mass persuasion through the media, what could one expect from the re-broadcast of such speech or political rally as we just saw?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a fundamental principle of effectiveness of propaganda is repetition. So the more often you repeat the same thing in speech, in -- visually, or you -- you actually symbolically re-enact something, the more persuasive it becomes. Again, absent some kind of a organised opposition that tells you that there are other ways of dealing with this -- with these issues. So, yes, repetition, re-broadcast, rephrasing, these are known and very effective tools of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to move into evidence the last clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, just an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to apologise if I did not hear this right. Could Ms. Dahl please repeat the date of this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was the 14th of April, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a lie, Judge. This is the well-known rally in Loznica against the blockade of Republika Srpska that was imposed by the Milosevic regime. This is a speech from 1995, when Republika Srpska was under a blockade. I am leading a mass of people to symbolically break through that blockade. You see what the Prosecution is resorting to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, what about the date? There must be a mistake. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm relying on the records I've prepared, Your Honour. I will do some research afterwards and submit the report to the Chamber in support of -- if we can mark that for identification for the time being, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. An MFI number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly, sir, just a follow-up question. We have just seen two video-clips in which there is a political -- a politician meeting with people, shaking hands, being applauded, making a speech. Nowadays these images can be seen anywhere in the world. We have politicians meeting prospective voters. They get applause. They shake hands, and their words are basically the same as the one we have just heard. So my question, because I do not want to be a victim of any kind of propaganda either: What kind of inference do we have to draw with regard to the media today, in this modern day and age? I mean, 1992, that's not the Middle Ages, is it? Is that a usual technique for a politician who is on tour who is holding speeches? As far as you can see, is that something that is to be condemned? Is it normal? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course this is what politicians do. They go on tour. They make speeches. But I think I've also pointed out to you that when you're talking about France or -- or Germany or Britain or Switzerland, and so on, there's a political opposition that also goes on tour. They also have speeches before audiences. Their message is broadcast on all kinds of channels, media channels. And the people who these messages are addressed to have all this other information coming to them. But in this particular case, as I've indicated to you, the -- pretty much 90 per cent of especially the television coverage was really just on the nationalist side. In -- in Republika Srpska, it was actually 100 per cent, because they shut down the TV transmission towers for the -- for the -- for the Bosniaks altogether. So we're in a very different situation from this deliberative discourse, where you see -- you're exposed to, so to say, all sides. The other thing I would point out to you is that what Dr. Seselj suggests by walking across this international border and -- and essentially symbolically saying it doesn't exist because the Greater Serbia does not recognize these -- these -- these boundaries, it would be very unusual for a German Chancellor to walk into Strasbourg and declare that the border of Alsace is different -- the border between France and Germany is different and Alsace already now somehow reverts back to or should revert back to Germany, instead of being part of France. And that's sort of the equivalent of what is being done here. So I don't think any Western politician in this democratic setting would do such a thing, and it would be really looked upon as ridiculous and absurd, as unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would it be considered a -- a provocation or an aggressive move internationally?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the audience, both in Republika Srpska and in -- and in Serbia, has been exposed to these messages now for four, five years, and for them it's pretty much par for the course. There's nothing surprising any more about it. So would it be considered provocative for the -- for the Bosniaks? Yes, extremely provocative, if you declare that the country really doesn't exist, doesn't have any borders any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let's turn now to a video-clip of a volunteer after the fall of Vukovar. This is 65 ter exhibit number 6032.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which date, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I have this dated after the fall of Vukovar, November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] This is rather unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm pulling the wrong one. This is before the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I'm a mother of two small children. Where are you from if. From Pirot. Who old are you? 33. Well, when I watch television, I see what's going on and I want to help. And it's worth sacrificing my life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, this is footage from Belgrade, not from Vukovar. This really makes no sense. It's all wrong, what the Prosecutor is doing. This is the departure of volunteers from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I introduced it incorrectly. This is from a documentary film about Vukovar that depicts the departure of volunteers from Belgrade before the fall. Mr. Seselj is correct. I have another clip about volunteers in Vukovar after the fall, which comes up next. So let me begin again. This is 65 ter exhibit 6032.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one remark. You are speaking about volunteers. We have just seen a lady who seems to be the mother of two children, who's 32 or 33 years old. She doesn't say that she's a volunteer from such-and-such a group. This is just what I wanted to point out to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I make a statement? She is dressed in a military outfit which the volunteers actually dressed in. She's not dressed in street clothes. She's not going there to do some -- to take her children to school. I mean, she's boarding the bus that the volunteers are taking to Belgrade. That's why Madam Prosecutor said that she's a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me -- let me play the clip again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not waste time, Judge. Let's not waste time. This really is a volunteer, a volunteer of the Serb Radical Party. That, this woman is, and I'm not challenging it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] This is rather unusual. A young woman going to war. Is it or isn't it? What do you think about that? I don't think it is. We need to answer the call to arms. I'm a mother of two small children. Where are you from? I'm from Pirot. How old are you? 33. What made you decide to go? Well, when I watch television I see what's going on and I want to help and it's worth sacrificing my life for this here Serbia of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to move that clip into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, again, the problem is that there is no date here. You saw a clip of seeing off volunteers a few moments ago where I spoke. This is a sequel to that. And you saw in the first video-clip that there was an interruption and a part of my speech is cut off where I am telling the volunteers how they are supposed to treat prisoners of war, civilians, women, and children at the front line, where they fight. This was tendentiously omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The date of departure of this lady, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I will look in our evidence collection and see if I can get a more specific date. Often we've been able to obtain a video from outside sources, that is, segments, so I'll see if I can get more precise dates. And the next video-clip, I also don't have a more precise date. I'll see what I can find. It was from a documentary film maker who testified. It's related to material that's already been admitted to Dr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case. This is 65 ter exhibit number 6012, clip A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Chetnik, Chetnik, remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to put the three clips together as one exhibit, so I'd like to proceed to another clip from that video, clip B.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] From Nis, a Chetnik. Seselj's party. If you heard. We are liberating. The JNA is doing nothing, nothing. Well, the volunteers and Chetniks were sent in to the worst operations when it was necessary. At one stage they withdraw. We are left alone on the battlefield together with the locals. This was always Serbia and the communists -- Wait a second. And the communists, they laid down the borders in 1945 and all of this is their fault. Tito's generals are -- Tudjman is one of Tito's generals, Anton Tus is as well. Well, our aim was to defend Serbdom orthodoxy. As far as I'm concerned, what those people from the Tribunal in The Hague and the journalists -- as precisely what that meant -- well, they asked if I'd go. Yes, again, I would again defend Serbdom and orthodoxy. Those are goals higher than my single life. The Serbs were exposed to genocide there during the Second World War. Vukovar is a story unto itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The last clip in this composite exhibit is clip C.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] It will be Serbian, ours. There will no longer belong -- it will no longer belong to Ustashas. There will be no more fascists. We will no longer allow it. For 50 years we suffered it and didn't say a word. We waited and they hated us. It's enough now. It's the end. We can only fight with them. [In English] They kill our children. We have never seen the kid of two years old with head -- the head of the kid is on the pick, you know, and here the pick is on the kid's body. You know what that mean? Have you seen that? No? That people, we discuss? Never. Only fight to the end, to the last. The last bullet, the last Ustasha. You know? That's everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to focus on the ideas articulated by the people whose clips we just saw. Can you pull out some examples of where Dr. Seselj's message has been repeated or replicated in these individuals.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- they pretty much, so to say, repeat what he's been saying for -- at this time, for at least about a year, if not more, in terms of the victimhood of the -- of the -- of the Serbs, the threat that the others -- other groups represented to him, and linking that to -- to actual action, removing the threat by -- you see them armed there in Vukovar. They've been doing the fighting. So they translate these political ideas and -- and propaganda into action. And the -- the young woman who has the two children, the -- actually says that she saw what was happening in Vukovar on TV. Before that, we had a clipping of a -- of a man who was about, I think he said it was 57 years old, from Nis, and he also wanted to enrol in the fighting forces to -- you know, to save Vukovar because of what he had seen on TV. And that's -- that's kind of unusual that people -- women with small children and an older gentleman should want to become a volunteer in an -- a military operation. I mean, it -- it shows the effectiveness and the power of television in -- in persuading people. I might -- I might add that I just notice that in my report I also quote Dr. Seselj on the effectiveness of television. This is in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you are very quickly drawing conclusions. We've just seen the three sequences, A, B, and C, of clip number 6012. And you seem to infer and say that people are saying all this because Mr. Seselj gave all these speeches. When I listen to you -- while I was listening to you, I was wondering, what is the substance of what these people are talking about? They're talking about crimes that occurred during World War II, crimes committed by Ustashas. They must have -- Ustashas. They must have learned that maybe through Mr. Seselj, but maybe also through their family and school, education, history lessons. I don't know. We also see a so-called soldier talking about the head of a child, this and that. I mean, this is not Mr. Seselj who told him all this, about the head of a child. But you seem to immediately -- to automatically connect what you see on these videos to Mr. Seselj. And listening to you, I was trying to remember what happened in your country after September 11th. You know, where Fox News and CNN were interviewing people who were saying, Well, they were ready to take up arms and fight the terrorists. They weren't saying that they wanted to do this because they had heard the President's speech or a politician's speech. So on this testimony that we have on video, could you tell us what is -- what comes from -- what is the contribution of Mr. Seselj and what is the contribution of what they saw on TV. We would have to prove here, to demonstrate that the accused controlled the media and the TV. But you seem to put this aside and immediately, just automatically state that this is the consequences of his words, of the words of the accused. So could you please shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can't really separate the -- you know, the influence of a whole bunch of people who are using basically the same kinds of propaganda, nationalist ideas, proposals for action. There's -- there's a lot of them at this time. In fact, there's a lot of them on the Croat side as well. You know, from the -- from the other side. But what I'm -- what I am saying is that within this discourse of nationalism, Dr. Seselj actually has a lot of access and exposure in the mass media and he keeps repeating the same message and he has kind of, I would say, almost a privileged position, in terms of disseminating this message. It's true other people are also doing it. They also have access to the mass media. I don't think to the extent that Dr. Seselj did. And furthermore, we have seen from the clippings that he talks directly to the volunteers. So it's not just a question of the mass media. It's a question of personal relationship that he has. He talks to them before they board the bus to Vukovar; he talks to them when he visits Vukovar. They repeat what he has been saying and what they've been hearing. So, yes, the degree of proof that you wish that you could do in some kind of a science, a natural science, does not exist here. I -- I completely admit that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In Professor Seselj's discourse, when you studied his texts, did you find examples of conciliatory or willingness to compromise in his political objectives?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- there were a few passages that would -- that would indicate that. And in fact I've quoted some of them and I cited some of them, but they are definitely outnumbered and overwhelmed by the -- more of a no-compromise sort of position that he takes, on borders, on Greater Serbia, on the status of Serbs who live outside of Serbia, and on all things that have to do with the fighting and bringing it to an end. And I -- I can actually quote some numbers for you later on, if you wish, in my summary of the content analysis on precisely that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you when we take the break if you could put together the summary and then we'll return to that, because I don't want to take up the time --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- looking for the figures. In political discourse, is there a risk associated with taking a position of a compromise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I would like the registrar to tell us how much time the Prosecution has already spent. But you can continue. You can continue and I'll tell you how much time you've already spent. But continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me return to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In political discourse, is there a risk associated with taking a position of no compromise?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer it this way: That Dr. Seselj pretty much takes that position over the period that we -- that I examine his content analysis. Now, there -- there are other prominent political leaders at this time who started with the position -- the -- the kind of nationalist position and the -- the no-compromise position that Dr. Seselj took throughout this time, but when they realized that this was leading into civil war and all this armed conflict and -- and so on, they -- they drew back and they -- they changed their views. And they were much more willing to say, Well, maybe compromise is a good idea, because we don't want this kind of civil war. And his rival, Vuk Draskovic, was one of these people. At -- at one time he was even a more -- in 1990, more popular nationalist fire brand than Dr. Seselj, and, of course, they were political rivals, but Vuk Draskovic, shortly after all these wars started, these killings started, sort of drew back and -- and changed his position on them, and he wanted a -- I don't say he became a pacifist, but he certainly became anti-war and he wanted to stop this whole -- you know, this whole development. So it's -- it's not an inevitable position. And at that time, taking a no-compromise, as Vuk Draskovic did change his mind on that, yes, it was a political liability, because the public by that time had become very nationalist and a substantial part of it was in fact for the war, but not all of them, of course, by any means. So yes, there was a political risk in -- in making this change.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And let me, as a matter of housekeeping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. For your information, Mrs. Dahl, you have used up three hours and 15 minutes. You have 30 minutes left. You could continue until 10.40 and end at 10.40, just before the break. So you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me move into evidence composite exhibit 6012, which is clips A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P21.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'd like to sum up your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to sum up your testimony, Dr. Oberschall. Can you present a summary of your -- the findings of your research.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, they -- they come on page 38 and 39 of my expert report. And I will summarise it now. That is, we've -- I've looked at, first, 244 media messages of Dr. Seselj in the years 1990 to 1994. And we looked at his view of relationship between Serbs and -- political relationships between Serbs and non-Serbs in this -- during the Yugoslav crisis. Now, he emphasised the victimisation of Serbs by other peoples and states and -- and outside states in ex-Yugoslavia, foreign states, international organisations. There are 40 victimhood and victimisation of Serbs' messages in the total of 242. He mentioned and repeatedly mentions that Serbia is threatened and surrounded by enemies, foreign states, neighbour peoples, even internal traitors who are Serbs, all of whom want to weaken the Serb state and the Serbs by dismantling the territory of Serbia and diminishing numerically the -- the Serb people. There are 42 threats against --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judge, there's no point in having the witness read -- read his report, if he can speak freely or interpret or tell us something new, but it really makes no sense to him to read the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please try to answer the questions and really give us a summary of the conclusion, as Mrs. Dahl asked, not read your report. We've read your report. We -- Mr. Seselj read it. I read it. We've all read it. But for the transcript, please summarise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason I'm referring to is simply that the content analysis I did is actually quantitative. It mentions numbers. I can't remember all these numbers, you know, by heart. But let me just say there's extraordinary large number of victimhood and victimisation messages, threats against Serbs messages, no compromise on any kind of a conflict management of the political and -- and ethnic conflicts that exist at this time. There's some very vivid violent images and statements about action to be taken, like the amputation of Croatia; another favourite phrase of Dr. Seselj is "rivers of blood will flow," which is extremely, extremely violent. There's large doses of justification for coercion and violent actions, such as the "rivers of blood will flow." And there's a lot of mentions and -- and references to the Serbs being a glorious nation that has some kind of a privileged standing among all the other peoples of Yugoslavia, who somehow are artificial creations of scheming politicians and -- and history, and what have you, and have no -- and the Serbs having greater rights to create this Greater Serbia at the expense of these other peoples. And finally, there's a very heavy dose of misinformation, falsehood, I would say even outright lies, in the -- in the statements, messages that -- that I've examined, and, of course, that's very much-- the heart of propaganda is the misrepresentation of fact and history. And what it amounts to is a -- a justification for xenophobic nationalism and extreme actions and justifications for these actions and a rejection of non-violent conflict management of these political and -- and ethnic conflicts and the differences between these groups, which in fact occurred in -- at this time, where it was actually happening in the Soviet Union as it was falling apart, where except for one secession in Chechnya and one conflict in Nagorno-Karabagh, this whole big, huge empire separated into 17 states in a -- in a fairly peaceful fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you explain some more about the alternatives to a violent renegotiation of a constitutional framework that you studied and discussed in your report.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I repeatedly -- well, the -- the case of the Soviet Union is actually a very good example, because, first of all, the Serbs and the Russians considered themselves as allies and have throughout history, but they -- they handled the break-up of their countries, their states, in a very different way. Huge Russian minorities exist in the Baltic countries, in the Ukraine, in the Central -- in the Central Asian republics, in the same way that Serb minorities existed in Croatia and in -- in Bosnia. But the -- the peoples in the Soviet Union as they broke up into 17 -- I think it was 17 different states, decided not to re-draw every border that had existed since, really, the 1919 constitution of the Soviet Union, which if they had done what Dr. Seselj suggested and every other group would have done the same, of trying to re-draw the borders and expel people from one -- one place to another place to -- to match the new borders, it would -- you would have had about a dozen civil wars going on in the territory of the Soviet Union at the same time. But they didn't do this. And they settled the question of how to break up a state and the new constitutions and the rights of peoples living in them, regardless of whether they're minorities or majorities, in a totally different fashion, and by and large in a -- in a peaceful fashion. So there was this model that was actually going on at the same time as the break-up of Yugoslavia was going on, but there are other -- I would say there -- at this time also what was going on is the civil war in South Africa between the African National Congress and the government of South Africa was going on and had been actually going on for a decade. It was a violent kind of insurgency. There was tremendous animosity between the different groups and -- had actually been going on for -- for quite some time, yet the political leaders on both sides saw that instead of destroying their country, they had to sit down and come up with a new constitution that admitted the equality of all these racial and ethnic groups on an -- on the basis of equality and they reached a power-sharing deal. And South Africa is a well-functioning country right now. And I would say on a -- on a grade of difficulty, if -- if as an outsider you look at how difficult it is to make people live together peacefully, I would say South Africa would be a much more difficult case and internationally most of the people who were experts on Yugoslavia thought that, you know, the -- the Croats, Serbs, Muslims, and everybody would sort it out in a fairly peaceful fashion. That didn't happen. And certainly the Soviet Union was looked upon as a higher risk case than -- than Yugoslavia. So yes, I make these comparisons and I think their appropriate, because leadership, political leadership has a lot to do with what happens in a country.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We had talked yesterday about the term "xenophobic nationalism." Could you contrast and discuss in closing the notion of civic nationalism and what are the predicates regarding the treatment of ethnic and religious groups within the umbrella of civic nationalism.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- in civic nationalism as sort of the foundation of a state, you start with the individual who has some basic equal inalienable rights, compared to everybody else who lives in that territory. And building from that, if there are particular groups with a different language of religion or cultural tradition, depending on their size and how dispersed or concentrated they are, as, for instance, in Canada, the French -- the French-language people, the Quebecois, you create a federal state or you create an autonomous region, you give them cultural rights. You make sure that they're a political representation in the -- the federal legislature is -- is adequate. You give provisions in the constitution that prevent majority from changing these arbitrarily unless there's consent by a substantial part of the minorities. In other words, there are precedents available, the South African constitution, the -- there are many others, the Indian constitution, the -- right now, the North -- Northern Ireland Peace Agreement is also based -- on this -- on this idea. Now, Dr. Seselj advocates another -- and believe you me, there's nothing wrong with nationalism. It's how you -- how you implement it in terms of a constitutional structure, the political rights of minorities, and the equality of citizenship. But if you start with the notion that a nation is privileged and other groups are not because they're artificial or they haven't had a -- a medieval history of -- of -- of a state or they're not speaking a language that's different from some other language sufficiently to be a separate language, or any other criterion, this is another way of building a state, and no matter what you -- you do or say, you end up with a privileged group and other groups that are minorities which are threatened or at least concerned about what's going to happen to them within that. I might say that the -- the great proponent of -- and the first theorist of civic nationalism was a French historian who gave a famous lecture at the Sorbonne in 1882, "Qu'est-ce qu'une nation?", and a lot of our political theories and views about it come from this source, as elaborated and implemented in -- in different contemporary settings.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: So unless I've missed something in particular that you think that the Trial Chamber would need in addition to your written report, I will conclude my examination. I'm not recalling -- well, I think we did move everything that we played into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will now have a break, a 20-minute break. Mr. Seselj, regarding time, we will resume at ten to 11.00. We will go for an hour and a half, have another 20-minute break, and resume. Theoretically, until 2.45. You might not have your three hours and 45 minutes that you're entitled to. If you wish to use up the three hours and 45 minutes, we'll have to resume tomorrow. Our problem is that Judge Lattanzi will not be here tomorrow morning. So could you please be brief and short in your cross-examination as much as possible. We could finish on time and finish today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the best of my will, it's simply impossible. I have really have plenty of reasons for my cross-examination to last three hours, 45 minutes. And I also have the intention of requesting from you that those 20 minutes you owe to me from that day when you asked me to shorten my opening statement, my statement of the accused, you said, remember, that you would give me those 20 minutes some other time. I intended to ask for those 20 minutes now, because Mr. Oberschall is a very important Prosecution witness. So we will certainly have to work tomorrow, but I hope that your other colleague will be present tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But our other colleague will be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a correction for the -- the transcript. In line 9 -- I mean, page 9, line 9, I understand Judge Lattanzi said "the accused" and not "the witness." In the context, "I would like the accused not to get into useless controversies" and I'd like to verify the translation in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just been told by the registrar that we can move to Courtroom I but we might need 30 minutes. So we shall resume at 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have resumed our hearing. We're going to start with the cross-examination. I give the floor to Mr. Seselj. Please proceed. Your time starts now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I cannot hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I was saying to you that you can start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. While I get all my papers out, I'm going to put a preliminary question to Mr. Oberschall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oberschall, do you know that during the course of 1993 and 1994 I was violently opposed to Slobodan Milosevic and his regime?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during part of that, you and he became rivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not "during part of," from mid-1993 and throughout 1994. Let us be very specific on this. Of course, in 1995 and 1996 and 1997 as well. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in 1995, 1996, and 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was also against him. Nothing changed. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not really true. That is to say, you were divided on some things, but you were actually quite cooperative on other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of cooperation did we have from 1993 to 1998? Tell me specifically.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milosevic -- Milosevic and you divided on the question of essentially what to do about the Bosnian war. And he was responding to the sanctions which were -- which were hurting Serbia, and he wanted some kind of a settlement, which in fact occurred after end of 1995 in -- in Dayton. And, of course, you were opposed to that. You were opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is not an answer to my question. Mr. Oberschall, I want you to give specific answers to all my questions. My question is --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has answered the question. If Mr. Seselj is not satisfied with the answer, that is not a basis to berate the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the accused put a question to you on the conflict he had with Mr. Milosevic, and he wanted you to say what the reasons were, as far as you knew, for this opposition. That's a major point. Do you know that or don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that he asked the witness what kind of cooperation there had been, not so much the conflict but the cooperation between 1993 and 1998, what kind of cooperation was there between the accused and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically Milosevic and -- and his party and Dr. Seselj and the Radical Party were on the nationalist end of the political spectrum, and they were both opposed to the liberal democratic parties and forces that were contesting both of them, as a matter of fact. It didn't matter who was in power and what positions they had. The liberal democratic opposition contested this -- the Seselj/Milosevic part of the political spectrum. And Seselj and Milosevic agreed to -- however -- whatever differences they had amongst themselves, they -- they agreed to oppose the -- the liberal and the democratic parties, whatever they -- they had a number of different names and coalitions and -- and so on, which formed, and whatever you want to call it. They were opposed by the nationalists. There were these two really large political groups opposed to one another, whatever internal differences there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I want you to give a specific answer to my question, to tell me exactly what was this form of cooperation that existed between me and Milosevic from mid-1993 until the beginning of 1998. One specific form of our cooperation.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't come here to -- and I didn't review the -- the history of the political parties and -- and specific -- specific events. I didn't prepare for that, so I'm not prepared to answer any specific question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then I'm right, when I say, Mr. Oberschall, that you have no idea about political developments in Serbia during those years; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. In fact, in my expert report I cite the -- the studies that have been done about election and election results, public opinion studies on precisely these questions of the nationalists versus the liberal democrats, and it's -- it's all in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your report now. A few moments ago here before the Trial Chamber you stated that in the period from 1993 until 1998, with regard to some questions I cooperated with Milosevic and I was divided on other questions. That is what you said here right now. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you have no idea whatsoever about anything specific that my cooperation with Milosevic during those years consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Objection. This is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, I'm trying to understand your answer with regard to the question put to you. First you said that from 1993 to 1998 Seselj and Milosevic did cooperate. The accused asked you in what regard there was cooperation, so this is a very specific question. Can you answer it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated to you, I didn't prepare for this -- for this -- for this examination or cross-examination a history of the political parties and relationships between Seselj, Milosevic, or anybody else during this period. A simple matter to -- to look it up and to, you know, go into the news reports, and so on, and analyses, but no, I don't have it on my fingertips. I've described to you the general politics at this time, which involved two blocs, whatever their internal differences. One is the nationalist and the other one is the liberal democratic side of the political spectrum. Now, the nationalists, whatever differences they had, they cooperated with one another, you know, opposing. They differed on foreign policy. They differed on some other matters. But they all agreed to oppose the liberal and the democratic bloc, in elections, in election coalitions, in running -- naming candidates. But no, I cannot name particular names and events which is what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I hope that somebody familiarised you here with the fact that I have the right to challenge your credibility as a Prosecution witness or Prosecution expert witness. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I stand corrected. It was a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpretation of Mr. Seselj's question appeared to not be a question until he concluded it with a fragment, so I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that Ms. Dahl is not going to do gymnastics here any more and just jump up at any point in time. She has to listen to things first and hear them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you understand me, Mr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask me questions, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. And I want to challenge your credibility as an expert. How can an expert state that from 1993 until 1998, I cooperated with Milosevic and cannot give a single indicator of that cooperation? Explain that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just did. First of all, I didn't say that from 1993 to 1998 you cooperated with Milosevic. That's not what I said. I said that during part of that time you were extreme rivals, actually, for political office. I also said that during other times -- I didn't say you cooperated on everything. I said that you saw eye-to-eye and you followed kind of the same political line, especially in how to handle and oppose the liberal democratic opposition in Serbia. And that's what I said, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, at the time when I was a university professor, when a student would in response to my direct questions give this kind of a nebulous answer, he would immediately be failed in that exam. That is what I did as a professor before I became a convict here in The Hague. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, this is improper cross-examination. Mr. Seselj is making a short speech that is not directed at Dr. Oberschall's testimony or credibility, and then asking him whether or not he agrees with that, that is improper, and I would ask that you instruct Mr. Seselj to direct his cross-examination in a way that moves the case forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say, Ms. Dahl, that I do not agree with your point of view. Mr. Seselj tackled the issue of credibility; therefore, regarding the issue of cooperation, he asked the witness what made him say that there was a cooperation between the accused and Milosevic, and the witness explained that he couldn't answer as to the merits and therefore he recognized, admitted that there were moments - this is what I can see in the transcript - when both were rivals. There's one thing I don't like. I don't like to have useless objections that are a waste of time. We, the Trial Judges, will have to make a final determination on the contents of the report. Objections are a waste of time, and you won't find any trace of them in the final judgement. So I do invite all to only raise objections when they are necessary. We are now at a stage when the accused is assessing or checking the credibility of the witness. Let him ask the questions. When Mr. Seselj calls his witnesses, you'll do the same. Anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, it was unclear. My objection concerned the accused's recollection of what he did when he was a university professor and whether he would fail a student for giving a nebulous answer. That was my objection to that particular question, not the other ones to which you referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please continue and tell us. What you were doing when you were a university professor, it might be interesting, but not so much here. Yes, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I give a specific example of -- of cooperation, which actually is mentioned in my expert report, and I believe it was in the election of 1996 when Dr. Seselj, I believe, was running -- I don't know if it was for president of Serbia or the whole of the federation, but at that particular moment he was given full access to the Serb television and the Serb media and he actually got a majority of the votes but not a -- a plurality of the votes but not a majority of the votes. But then there was a falling-out between the two of them and the Milosevic party decided to run a candidate against Dr. Seselj from their own party. His name was Milutinovic, I believe. I'm quoting from memory. And at that point, because the -- because the Milosevic regime wanted Milutinovic to win, they cut off access to television to Dr. Seselj, and in fact they did a lot of negative political coverage on TV, and this was only three weeks between these two elections, and he lost something like -- I don't know the exact number. Something like 20 to 40 per cent of his previous votes were now diminished and went to Milutinovic. So when they cooperated, three weeks later they didn't cooperate. This is sort of a good example also of the effects that rivalry, versus cooperation, has in terms of the influence on -- on -- on the -- on the voters in Serbia. That's -- to me that's a good example. And you have the details and the exact numbers are actually in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, obviously you have no idea, do you? In 1996, there were no presidential elections. What presidential elections are you talking about in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can go into the report and dig out the exact date for the election. And as I said to you, I wasn't sure whether it was elections for the Presidency of Serbia or for the Presidency of the whole federation. There were many elections at this time. In any case, it was a crucial election in which you were -- ended up running against Milutinovic. And when the Serb media, which were controlled by Milosevic, were shut off and reported on you negatively, you lost -- again, the exact numbers are in my report. It was between 20 and 40 per cent votes. You got less votes. And there was only three weeks before -- between the two elections. And that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I am saying that you have no idea whatsoever. In 1996, there were no presidential elections.
