However, presidential elections were held in 1997, presidential elections in Serbia, that is. What is an example of cooperation for you at these presidential elections? The fact that I had access to the media, state media, independent, pro-Western, is that a form of cooperation that would be an example?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any time that a regime allows political leaders to have access to the state media that it controls, that's definitely a form of cooperation. I mean, all the testimony here was how powerful the effects of television are on influencing people, so access is definitely a form of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you are avoiding an answer to my question. If the presidential elections in France, the candidate of the regime and the candidate of the opposition have access to the media, to state media and private media, is that a form of cooperation between the regime and the opposition in France, or is that something that is natural and normal and that has to be allowed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the political regime and system of France and of Serbia at this time were very different, and the difference being that in a democratic country the opposition has access to the state media and also other media; whereas, that was not the case in the -- in the -- in the Serbia that we're talking about in the middle 1990s. And I've indicated in my testimony that studies done at the Institute of Political Studies in Zagreb, in Belgrade, by -- by Serb researchers indicated that about 90 per cent of access to television was completely controlled by the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, do you know who else was an opposition candidate at the presidential elections in 1997 except for me -- or rather, in addition to myself?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I -- I mention it in my report, and it's a simple matter of looking it up. I think his name was Lilic, but I'm not sure. There were others. There was a whole -- you know, if you -- if you -- excuse me. I haven't finished yet. If you want to get all this detail, there's a -- an authoritative book published by Goati on all the elections in Serbia at this time, and they will list exactly who ran, what votes they got, whether they were a legislative or a -- or a presidential election, and all the different circumstances surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, although you are 20 years older than I am, I have still read more books than you have. Do not direct me to literature. Give me a direct answer. Who in addition to myself was an opposition candidate in these elections?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your answer was Zoran Lilic. Zoran Lilic was a regime candidate. He's a member of Milosevic's party, and Milosevic made him run for president because Milosevic moved to another post before that. You have not answered me. You have not given me an answer because you don't know. Let us move on. You're wasting a lot of my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of the elections, the elections that took place on the 5th of October, 1997, you say that he got 1.734.000 votes. Lilic, his opponent, got 1.475.000 votes. The accused Seselj has just said that he at the time was the candidate for the opposition, whilst Lilic was Milosevic's candidate. Now, are these results in compliance with what you say? Because since he was a candidate for the opposition, he could not control the media, could he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wasn't a candidate for the liberal democratic opposition. As I said, the nationalist bloc had a majority of the votes, so oftentimes when they ran the top person might be a Radical Party person; the second one would be a -- one from Milosevic's party; and the other candidates would come in third, fourth, or fifth; and then there would be a run-off between the two top candidates, who were rivals, yes, but they were in the same nationalist bloc. So it wasn't like a -- one nationalist running against one liberal democrat, but two competing nationalists running against one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I insist that you give me an answer. In these presidential elections, who was a candidate of the liberal democratic opposition, as you've been calling them? Did the liberal democratic opposition have a candidate of its own? Did they?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at -- at various times they ran candidates for -- at different levels, the Assembly, the Presidency, the Belgrade Municipality. You know, there was a number of -- a different number of them, and different times they formed different coalitions of liberal democratic parties. Again, I don't see how the history of the internal politics of Serbia after 1994, which is the period that ends my content analysis, has really anything to do with what this Court has been and I have been dealing with. If you're interested in the detail, you can look it up in all kinds of publications, which -- if I had known that Dr. Seselj was going to ask many questions about it, I would have looked it up and, you know, prepared myself for it. There's lots of things that I -- I have to consult before I can give an authoritative testimony about it. It's not in my mind currently all the time. I wouldn't expect anybody else to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, it is not my intention to gain knowledge from you. It is my intention to prove that you know nothing and that you are just speaking off the top of your head. Just confirm that you don't know who the candidate of the liberal democratic opposition was in the presidential elections in 1997. You don't know; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can look it up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't have to look it up. You don't have to look it up. I'll tell you. It was Vuk Draskovic. He was excluded already in the first round. Who had more access to the media, state-owned, opposition, and the so-called independent? Vuk Draskovic or I, in the first round?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't seen any studies done on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is literature. There is data in the literature. Studies were made and they show that Draskovic had incomparably more access to the media than I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. Why don't you enter it into the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please focus your questions on the relevant period in the indictment. Here we're talking about 1997 elections. It might be very interesting, but the Bench is interested in what happened in 1991, 1992, 1993. Everything is interesting, of course, but we don't have much time, so please focus.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Judge, allow me to topple the credibility of this witness and then I don't even have to move on to that relevant period. When I have convinced you that this witness has no credibility at all, why would I question him further? He said twice that I cooperated with Milosevic from 1993 to 1998, and he was unable to produce a single detail. It's not my fault. I'm looking for his weaknesses, and I'm trying to topple him completely as a witness and as an expert. Let me do it the way I conceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, according to me, you're entitled to challenge the quality of this witness as an expert. You have this right, but it only deals with the relevant period, from 1992 -- 1991 to 1994, if I'm right. So he could be an expert, if you cannot succeed in your endeavour -- he could very well be an expert of that period and not an expert of the following period, which is why the Presiding Judge just asked you to focus on the relevant period. Thank you. And please comply with what I have just said and what the Presiding Judge has just said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, thank you too for this caution, but I want to draw your attention to the fact that I have the right in cross-examination to test the credibility of any witness or expert, also on the basis of facts that concerned his primary school education. Everything is possible there. I don't need to tell you that I have a precious precedent. The way of cross-examination in the trial against Oscar Wilde. I haven't yet reached that degree. Maybe at some point I will. It won't be needed, however, for Mr. Oberschall and I don't need to be cautioned in this way. Mr. Oberschall has already shown that he's talking off the top of his head, without really knowing the facts. That's why I'm testing his credibility and challenging it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the first round, Lilic got the most votes. I was in second place. Draskovic was cast off as the third. So in the run-off, there was Lilic and I. What -- do you know what happened later, after that, Mr. Oberschall, when the socialists put up Milan Milutinovic as a candidate?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really is -- concerned the -- a time period that is not covered by my content analysis and the Honourable Judge has actually said that you should not really ask me questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. That means that you don't know that a special envoy, Mr. Gelbard from the US came to Belgrade and told Milosevic that all means are permissible against Seselj. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's of no interest to me whatsoever. I have nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. It's no interest to you. But do you know that the envoy in Belgrade, thanks to American support, agreed to falsify the results of elections when the main candidates were Milan Milutinovic and I. Do you know that? With the American support, the elections were falsified.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you claim that, and, of course, you can say a lot of things. You -- you, in fact, said that politician engages in propaganda and it's full of lies, and it's very hard to tell when you're telling the truth or when you're making propaganda. So if you want to document that and introduce it to the Court, or whatever the -- the procedure here is, that's fine with me, but I have no comment on, you know, these kind of rumours and opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, it's a notorious fact in Serbia and any of your associates from Belgrade could have told you that, if you had made the inquiry. But let us leave that aside. In your report here, you dealt with the issue of propaganda and you gave a narrow definition of "propaganda" as a technique of persuasion, calling on emotion. Do you know that propaganda, among other things, is also a means of political manipulation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a -- it's a technique of -- of -- of political persuasion and -- and manipulation based on a disregard of facts and -- and the truth. And I -- actually, I gave that definition, I think, on page 2 of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please give me brief answers, because time is precious to me. Do you know that in 1994, for violations of parliamentary procedure by the president of the Federal Parliament, several incidents occurred in the Assembly of Yugoslavia, the Federal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what incidents are you referring to? There are a lot of incidents happening all the time in the Federal Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I mean 1994, when after several such incidents I was arrested. And sent to gaol for four months. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is -- is that the incident where you attacked a journalist and -- and threatened him, or is that another incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did I attack a journalist in the Assembly? Please don't make things up. It was an incident involving the security detail in the Parliament when the president of the Parliament ordered that one of our MPs be thrown out after that MP had poured water on the Speaker of the Parliament. You know that. That's the incident I'm talking about. You were in Belgrade three times. This is still the subject of many stories.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- I wasn't in Belgrade to collect stories about anything. I'm -- I mean, I'm -- I'm doing real research. And I was in Belgrade only once, and this particular incident and what you did and what you didn't do with a journalist, that wasn't the -- you know, my main concern. I was -- I was much more concerned with the much broader picture of collective violence in Croat-Serb war, in the Bosnian situation, and how to resolve these differences through some kind of a peaceful means. That was the focus of my research, and not particular speeches you made or didn't do or what you said to journalists, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. In your report, you stated that I was a significant political leader. If I was that significant, then the fact must be also significant that from end September 1994 until end January 1995, I was in Milosevic's gaol. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that brief answer. Are you aware that the Milosevic regime in 1994 imposed the blockade on Republika Srpska, possibly with a "yes" or "no." Preferably with a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were debates and proposals and issues that had to do with how Milosevic was going to influence or even coerce the Republika Srpska to follow his kind of way to resolve the Bosnian war. Yes, there were such discussions going on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware that in the spring of 1995, when I got out of prison, I convened a rally in Loznica to protest this decision of Milosevic's? You saw that rally some time ago earlier today.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we showed that rally on the TV or monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And after that rally, we marched to the Drina River. There were around 10.000 people, and that was shown as well. Let us just note that, and then I'll ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't contest this. Milosevic sent 1.000 special policemen to the Drina River to stop us, but when they saw our numbers, the police divided their ranks to let us through. Now, here's the question: You saw a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I really don't know how many policemen Milosevic may have sent or -- or were there. I -- I just simply don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never mind. Maybe there were 980. The number doesn't matter. This is the question: You were a witness here that the Prosecutor was showing this video-clip, claiming that it was footage from 1992. Is this an obvious example of propaganda-driven manipulation, political propaganda manipulation for the purpose of extorting a conviction in this trial? Answer that.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have a more simple common-sense interpretation that when one handles a lot of documents, occasionally one makes a mistake in terms of numbers and dates and -- but that gets rectified when it's -- when it's noted, and that happens in any kind of a proceeding, judicial or -- or otherwise. So I don't see anything sinister about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as an academic, you should know that science fears conclusions based on common sense. Conclusions based on common sense often led science astray. You know that as an academic.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'm not prepared here to debate with you about the philosophy of -- of science and such other matters. I wish you would concentrate on the work I've done on content analysing your speech, which is what I came to -- to testify about, and not to talk about the philosophy of science. I mean, I'd like to do that in a cafe after these proceedings are over, but I don't see any purpose in doing that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you are a Doctor of Philosophy, you have a Ph.D. in philosophy, don't you? Am I right? Why are you avoiding a philosophical debate in the part of cross-examination when I'm testing your credibility? We both have a Ph.D., and as a much more capable, more educated man, I am testing your credibility. That's my entitlement.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. If you want to use up your time and discuss with me the philosophy of science, I'm glad to do that. This is actually an interesting topic, but that's not what I'm here for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Oberschall, I asked where were you born, and you're telling me when you were born.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Budapest, 1936.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your citizenship. By ethnicity, are your -- are you a Hungarian or something else? What is your origin?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The origin -- by origin, I'm Hungarian. Right now I'm an American.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is your citizenship, but your nationality is Hungarian. That doesn't matter really today, but I finally got an answer to that as well. In 1958 you majored in physics, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in 1962 you got a Ph.D. in sociology.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Isn't that a bit unusual that somebody who majored in physics should then go on to get a Ph.D. in sociology?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Actually, my advisor, who actually created the whole field of mass communications, whose name was Paul Lazarsfeld, had his first degree in Vienna in -- in physics and -- and he became a sociologist, and I studied under him. So there is nothing unusual about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What requirements did you have to meet in order to get that Ph.D. in sociology?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to take a certain number of -- of courses in the graduate faculty at Columbia university, some of which were the ones that I'm using now in my position here as an expert witness on mass communications, content analysis. We also had to get certain grades in these -- in these courses. We had to write a Ph.D. dissertation. We had summer training in various research -- on various research projects. And those are the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is the subject of your Ph.D. dissertation? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject of my Ph.D. dissertation is on the history of social research on -- in -- in Germany in the latter part of the nineteen and early twentieth centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While you were studying physics, you also read certain subjects related to maths, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To -- to what? To ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mathematics. In studying physics, you also studies mathematics. Mr. Oberschall, do you know what an imaginary number is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sure. We call them complex -- functions of complex variables. Yes, they're -- they're used to solve certain equations in the calculus. So what, are we going from the philosophy of science to mathematics now, Mr. Seselj, Dr. Seselj? I mean, what is this getting to? I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm showing that you don't know what an imaginary number is. An imaginary number is the root of a negative number. For instance, the root of 4 -- the square root of 4 is 2; whereas, the square root of minus 4 cannot be 2. It's written as 2i in mathematics. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. Complex numbers are --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, that's not what you said. You don't know it, so you try to... Just one more question from physics. Do you know what Avogadro's number is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know. And which number of atoms are contained in 1 gramme of any element? 1 gramme of mass in any element?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know. Fine. So we see that you are no physicist and then you had to move on so sociology. Let's move on. Mr. Oberschall --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I make an interjection here? May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, you cannot until I ask you a question. When I ask you a question, then you will be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oberschall, go ahead. Do your interjection. Maybe you're a bit surprised by these questions, but this is a adversarial procedure, common law, so Defence has the right to ask questions to check the credibility of a witness using the resume provided by the Prosecution, and on your resume I see that you have a -- in 1958 you obtained a physics bachelors and then a sociology in 1962, a sociology degree in 1962, and so the accused is trying to check that your diplomas do correspond to something. If they don't correspond to anything, he may challenge your technical competence. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I have to say is that Dr. Seselj has a very different view of what learning and education is really all about. He seems to think that a whole bunch of facts that are memorised constitute knowledge. And in fact when he started asking me questions about Serb politics in the, you know, 1990s, and so on, he also seems to think that just memorising a whole bunch of facts is what we refer to as "knowledge"; whereas, what they teach you at my university, Harvard University, where I got a doctorate in physics, is a way of thinking the main principles of a discipline. And then they tell you if you're interested in looking up certain facts, Here are the handbooks. Here are the sources that you go to. And those facts keep changing as science advances. So his way of testing my knowledge is sort of old-fashioned early nineteenth century stuff and not contemporary philosophy of science and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will take note of this. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I just wanted to note that Mr. Seselj's examination is not a traditional adversarial common-law cross-examination, not any that my training and background make me familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please, go to the point. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Judge, that this extensive monologue by Mr. Oberschall will be deducted from the time available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These are basic categories without which one cannot speak about any knowledge in physics, not even methodology of physics is possible without knowing this. Mr. Oberschall, when did you get the assignment from the Prosecution to prepare your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been several years. I -- I forget now. Maybe three and a half years. It's been a long time, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't matter particularly. You probably drew up some sort of contract with them, I suppose, about your expertise, or was it an order? What was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they asked me whether or not I was competent to do a content analysis of your -- of your statements, speeches, and all of the material that I've in fact content analysed, and I said yes. I know -- I know how to do this. I know how to do this. I've written about the break-up of Yugoslavia, the Bosnian war especially, so I -- I had some knowledge of the subject matter. And -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I'm not testing your credibility any more. Now we are doing something different. No need to justify yourself. I want to know what kind of material and what volume of material the Prosecution provided you with at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I agreed to do this and they agreed that I should do it, they sent me CD-ROMs of all your published -- or some of your published, not all of your published, volumes which were available in that form. And that's sort of the raw material from which the content analysis was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And since it wasn't translated into English, I had to hire a -- a Ph.D. candidate, a graduate student, Miss Bela Marovic -- Bela Maric. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stated that in the report. No need to repeat. At that time, did the Prosecution give you a text numbering 400 pages titled "Notification by Dr. Seselj of Special Defence," from September 2003? Did you get that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From September 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, September 2003. I provided that to the Prosecution as notification of my special defence, special form of defence. You didn't get that, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I got the indictment that the Court served on you, and I don't recall that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Oberschall. Yes, you do not recall because you did not receive it. Did you ever see my book "The Hague dossier of a war criminal -- or rather, a person blamed as a war criminal"? I'm showing it to you right now. You've never had this in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Now, why am I asking you this? I published that 400-page-long notification in this book because my associates in this paper collected an enormous number of my speeches where I ask for respect for international humanitarian law, proper behaviour towards prisoners of war, proper behaviour towards women, children, civilians, and so on. So they never submitted that to you; right? You never had this material in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only material that I was asked to examine --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, time is precious for me. Please, please, I know what you got. You told me. But you never got this; right? Now I'm interested in what it is that you did not get, not in what you did get. You see? This is not against you. You don't have to make excuses for yourself. You don't have to defend yourself. Let us move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be able to answer the question that was put to him. I believe, if the translation is correct, that Mr. Seselj interrupted the witness's opportunity to answer the question what material he was asked to examine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked to examine material that related to Serb/non-Serb political relations during the period 1991-1994. I was not asked to examine what your ideas were on agricultural policy, on the tariffs, on other kinds of other things, what you thought about the Court, and -- and many other topics, I'm sure, on which you have spoken and written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, it seems that you don't understand this procedure. Never mind. I don't hold it against you at all. And all of this is not against you. This does not throw any negative light on you, what I'm going to ask you right now. Did the Office of the Prosecutor make available to you three papers that I submitted dealing with hate speech in the West, hate speech by different Western statesmen and journalists, in Croatia and in the Muslim part of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you ever receive these three papers? I also handed that in as a form of special defence. This was done by Dejan Mirovic, one of my experts, with a group of co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we ask Mr. Seselj to be more specific with regard to the document references, for instance, what date he submitted them, because I'm not able to identify that without some specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, could you be more specific as to these papers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, you have them in an abbreviated form, the one that I submitted as requested by you, in terms of special defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I received from you and I read very carefully is sort of a 160-page rejoinder that you and your research staff gave to my expert report. And in that rejoinder there's a great deal of material that you've just described about hate speech, about -- so I -- I know -- whether or not it's the particular papers, I have that. I've looked at it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No. You got my first rejoinder to your expert report, but you did not get the addendum to the second part of your expert report. I submitted that on the 26th of November, 2007. There is no way you could have received that; right? But I'm not asking you about that. I'm talking to you about three expert reports or papers on hate speech. You never received that. What about my book "The Vatican anti-Serb instrument Franjo Tudjman"? That's a book of mine. It's 1.000 pages long. Did you have that in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't. Don't be afraid. I don't think you had it. Anyway, in this book I published this paper about hate speech in Croatia in the relevant period. You did not have that in your hands and you could not compare that to the excerpts from my speeches that you provided your expertise on. Mr. Oberschall, did you ever have in your hands my book "The American anti-imperial instrument Alija Izetbegovic"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Anti-Serb instrument. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It deals with hate speech by Muslim politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina and their media, the thesis being that it is far more pronounced on their part if there is any on my part. I don't hold it against you. If nobody gave it to you, nobody gave it to you. Mr. Oberschall, did the Prosecution provide to you three papers of mine on special defence in which on 4.000 pages I deal with the thesis that it was the Popes of Rome, John Paul II and Benedict XVI are the main culprits for the war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and they are the guiltiest of all for all the war crimes that took place. Now never got that; right? Let me cut things shorter for you and make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm really grateful I didn't get it, because, you know, I read other fiction, not this kind of thing that you write.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, so that is fiction that the Popes are the main criminals? You consider that to be fiction? You consider that to be fiction? Mr. Oberschall, did you ever have in your hands my book "The devil's apprentice, the criminal Pope John Paul II"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Oberschall, did you ever have in your hands "Pontifex Maximus of the Satanist church, John Paul II." Did you ever see that book of mine?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever have in your hands "The Anti-Christ apostle, Benedict XVI"? No? You never had that in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever have in your hands my book "Rome always thirsty for Serbian blood"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, did you ever have in your hands my book "The Vatican, the nest of Satan"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of those books I've had. I'm sure you have a lot of those books. None of them I've had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did not have any one of my books in your hands? Not a single one?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the ones that were sent to me on the CD-ROMs, which, were, I think, the 41 volumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you say that my accusations against the Vatican and the Popes of Rome are fiction, and, of course, you do not know that in these books I published papers on special defence in which I collected scientific analyses of foreign - that is to say, Italian, French, English, American, and other authors - and Serbian authors about the criminal role played by Popes of Rome. You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, since, you know, we are both Ph.D.s and we're both ex-professors, I'd like to know whether the Vatican opened its archives to your researchers so that, you know, you could extract all of that information to -- to make a case. Did the -- did the Vatican open its archives to you so that you could do research on what they really did? I mean, I -- I'd like to know that. It's -- it's -- it would be a very interesting development in the way the Vatican handles its -- its archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I'm the one who's putting questions to you, not you to me. However, since I find you to be a very likable man, I am going to answer you. It's not that my researchers researched this. They drew on the books of most renowned world authors. They got the relevant portions and they created a volume of 4.000 pages; Elena Bozic-Talijan and Zoran Krasic did that. And the OTP has had this material for the past two years. However, this is just for the sake of your information. Since you did not read any one of my books in their entirety, you certainly did not read the book entitled "The ideology of Serb nationalism"; right? It has over 1.000 pages. It's over 1.000 pages long.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this could have been one of the books that was on these CD-ROMs that we actually examined. I'm not sure. I mean, I don't have the memory of all these titles in my -- in my head. But if it -- if it relates to events between 1991 and 1994, in terms of your political activities, then we probably had that book. I mean, I don't have in memory 41 titles --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know why this book is important? This book does not talk about my political activities. It supports from a scientific point of view my assertions regarding historical facts that you consider to be untrue in your expert report. I am drawing on sources here, well-founded sources. That is the core of the matter. And now I see that you haven't seen that. What about "The Roman Catholic criminal project of the artificial Croatian state," that book of mine? Have you ever had a look at that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. Mr. Oberschall, in that book, on 1.000 pages - and I wrote it as I was sitting in prison here over these past five years, here in The Hague - I proved scientifically that present-day Croats are an artificially created nation on the part of the Catholic Church. And in one sentence in your report you say that is not true. You did not go into the arguments that I presented at all. In your view, it is impossible for the Popes of Rome to be criminals. And I am presenting evidence to the effect that for the past 1.000 years the Popes of Rome were as a rule criminals, including this Pius XII or whatever, who is called a criminal even in science. Now, what am I proving to you through this? Mr. Oberschall, I am showing to you that we are worlds apart, we are two different worlds. You are burdened with stereotypes, and for you the Pope is something positive. Are you Catholic, Mr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, put a question. The way I read what you have just said is a statement, rather than a question, so based on the books you have written, put questions so that he can answer and say whether he knows or not. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The question I put was whether Mr. Oberschall is a Roman Catholic, in terms of his religious background. I have the right to put that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think he's out of bounds here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I have no problem answering that I don't practice any religion whatsoever. I mean, I'm a secular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. That's an answer too. I'm not opposed to that. That is your conviction. But I was interested in knowing. Mr. Oberschall, now up until the break, since I used up a lot more time than I had planned to, we are going to deal with a question from this last addendum of yours that I received on the 7th of December. This is the addendum to your report. On page 1, you respond to my first official notification regarding your report, and you say -- and you are right on that -- that among the categories that you codified, there is no category of hate speech. Right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that the indictment against me is based to a considerable degree on me having committed grave war crimes through hate speech?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's not my business. I'm an expert here to -- it's not for me to decide what the indictment says or doesn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm doing the content analysis. Hate speech -- excuse me, I haven't finished. Hate speech is used in the -- in the media and in conversations in a very vague unspecific way. And if you're going to do a serious content analysis, you have to be much more precise about exactly what you're saying and what the content is. And that's why I produced the categories at the -- that you can read, that we have read, for -- for the content analysis, and that's how I -- I coded you. My testimony here yesterday and even in the beginning of today very strongly indicates that as far as social psychology and social science is concerned, threat speech is what is really important in getting people to act. You raise a consciousness of threat against a group that creates fear and anxiety and the demand for action, and usually hate comes after horrible actions have been committed and it makes conciliation conflict management more difficult when people hate each other. But the crucial part of the propaganda that sets in motion actions is actually the threat speech. And I've illustrated with particular statements, through video-clips, and also in the content analysis that your nationalist rhetoric was very heavily filled with threat speech. And so me, as an expert, that is the important part of-- of -- of how to explain actions that are hostile, aggressive, violent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, there is no need to provide these long explanations that are no answer to my question. Do you know that the Council of Europe gave a specific definition of "hate speech"? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know what the Council of Europe's specific definition of "hate speech" is. I've looked at some of what US law and British law says, but the Council of Europe, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know -- well, you'd have to know about that as an expert. You were supposed to read up on that, but I'm not going to teach you. Do you know about British jurisprudence and how hate speech was brought into it as a category?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was an extensive debate on that in the House of Lords with regard to that law that dealt with hate speech. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- you refer recently to the -- the -- still during the Blair government's introduction of a bill in parliament. It was about 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that -- because there was debate on exactly what is hate speech and what is incendiary statements. And Lord Hoffmann in the House of Lords actually made a very impassioned plea in opposition to the Blair government's position. I know that debate. I don't know what debate you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But the first debate was in the 1980s, and that is when hate speech was restricted only to racial hatred. And it was defined that hate speech can constitute -- or rather, hate speech can, for example, be a differentiation between and among races, saying that one race was superior to another, and that is prohibited, that kind of hate speech. That is from the 1980s. In America, too, as far as I know, that is what all this insistence is based on; that is to say, to make hate speech punishable. Right? So hate speech is not a threat. Hate speech is not aggression. It is an attempt to make a biological distinction between and among races, saying that one race is superior to another. That is the experience of Hitler's Germany. Are you aware of that? You're not a lawyer and you do not really know about legal categories, do you? Mr. Oberschall --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not here as a lawyer and I'm not here to -- to make -- give judgements or make -- give my testimony about legal distinctions and categories. I'm not here for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oberschall, the accused asked a question that may prove relevant in this case. You may be able to answer it, or not. That's his -- that's what he says, of course. The Trial Chamber will check. But he says that the hate speech, in his view, aims at making a biological differentiation based on races and it has nothing to do, he says, with a speech in which there is a content of threat. Do you agree with him or not, or are you not in a position to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been true in the -- in the 1980s, but what -- what is hate speech in more recent legislation, both in the United States and in Britain, and maybe elsewhere too, involves other elements. But I'm not -- I'm not an expert in the history of hate speech and how it has been defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us be more specific on this. This kind of a definition of hate speech did exist before the recommendation of the Council of Europe a few years ago. Let's be clear on that. So the recommendation of the Council of Europe made this very specific, but I was already in prison by then if I remember correctly. When you analysed parts of my texts, you specified that I deal with the glorification of an accepted group. Is that right? That is point number 1. In the American legal system, is that prohibited? What -- what is it that you bear in mind, the First Amendment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not prohibited --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your answers matter a lot to me, and it's not against you. You seem to be so defensive. I don't intend to attack you any longer. I had to attack you at first. Relax a bit now. But please give me specific answers to my questions. In the American legal system --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but working in three languages, as we are now, I need to try to protect our transcripts, and I would ask that Mr. Seselj be asked to allow enough time for translation before the question and answer continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Dahl, with regard to you, you have to do that, but, of course, the main warrants are the Judges, so that there's no confusion in the minds of those who may be listening to these proceedings. You say that there may be a problem regarding the transcript? On what point exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the last several questions, I believe that Mr. Seselj is able to understand the witness's answer in English and so that -- he begins to talk before the transcript of Dr. Oberschall's answer is completed. And so I'm getting brackets in place of his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Mr. Seselj, let the witness finish before you start with another question; otherwise, it won't appear in the transcript. But please put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the American legal system, is it prohibited to deal with stereotypes when there is public speech by statesmen, journalists, other public speakers? Is that prohibited through criminal law, or is it only subject to scholarly criticism?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, you seem to be under the -- under the false impression that I am trying to abridge free speech, your free speech, or any political free speech. All of these things that I've listed here that I'm content -- coding for content, "glorification, negative stereotyping, mention of internal threats, advocates and expects violence," these are all protected by free speech. I'm not -- I'm not making the argument that -- that your speech should be abridged or any such speech should be abridged. I'm not saying anything like that. That's not what my content analysis is about. And, in fact, I don't even have a category that says "hate speech." If you read my report, I specifically say -- I specifically say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically say that you do not use racial categories the way the Nazis did in your political discourse, and that is why I have -- even though I have the category "dehumanisation," which corresponds to that, I have not checked you off on any of your speeches in this category, because you simply are not falling into the Nazi kind of racial hate discourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, well, yesterday I commended you here. I said that you were precious to me as a Prosecution witness. Don't defend yourself any more. I am so sorry that I didn't get ahold of you before the Prosecution did. We would have had perhaps a more successful cooperation with regard to these matters. You are right. Don't defend yourself. Stereotypes are not prohibited. Now, threats, unless it's a threat to an individual person, say the gentleman saying next to me. Say I threaten him that I'm going to hit him or that I'm going to slap this other gentleman. No, if it's not a question of such individual threats, but general threats. For example, when the American President threatens to attack Iraq and he does attack Iraq and he kills 100.000 Iraqis, 200.000 Iraqis, and so on and so forth. These general threats, are they punishable by American law, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They're not. Thank you, Mr. Oberschall. We have this excellent cooperation. In the American legal system, is advocating violence prohibited? For example, the American President, President Bush -- Judge, let me just deal with this quickly and then I'm going to move on to something different after the break. When the US President, President Bush, advocates the bombing of Iran on false accusations, that Iran is making an atomic bomb, the intelligence agencies are saying that in 2003 Iran stopped working on this project. Is that advocating violence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it's advocating. Bombing is violence. But it's -- of course, it's not -- he's saying that's a possibility. He doesn't say it has to be done. But it's a possibility, an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we see, in using the example of Iraq, that this possibility was actually carried through, on the false accusation that Saddam Hussein has -- had weapons of mass destruction, Bush attacked Iraq, destroyed Iraq, killed hundreds of thousands of Iraqis, liquidated Saddam Hussein, and after that we find out that there were no weapons of mass destruction. Aren't these the actual facts?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not here to really talk about contemporary history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was an objection that was raised. Mr. Seselj, following your question, the Prosecutor is saying this is not relevant. Could you tell us what the relevance of your question is. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat the question briefly. Does the American legal system prohibit advocation of this type of violence? Is it forbidden for someone to appear on television and say Iraq or Iran should be bombed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not forbidden --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oberschall. I suppose you heard about Zbigniew Brzezinski advocating that Russia should be divided into three or four states. Do you know about this advocacy of his?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've followed Brzezinski -- he was actually one of my professors at Harvard. And I've followed his career and his pronouncements. I don't recall him saying anything like that. I don't know what it has to do with what we're doing here in this courtroom, but no, I haven't heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He published a book about that. But never mind. In the United States, is that kind of public advocacy of violent changes of state borders punishable? That's my question. For instance, if an American politician says that Iraq should be divided into three states: Kurdistan, Shiites Iraq, and Sunni Iraq?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer the question, and then we'll have a break. Right after the question -- you've heard the question, please answer it and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can advocate in American political discourse any kind of state change, boundary change, change in international relations, war policy, or -- or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please. One brief question. Just this one, please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the American system, in your opinion,, would I be able -- would I be held criminally responsible for any fragment, any passage from my speeches that you analysed? To the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- the context is important here. If you're in a war zone, there's armed conflict going on, civilians are being killed, and you make a speech to your men in which you say, you know, Continue, take, displace, get rid of them, instead of saying, Stop. That is to say, if you advocate violence in a dangerous situation where civilians, non-combatants, are at risk and are being killed, yes, then there's grounds for prosecuting you under existing law. If you say it on TV in a non-combat kind of situation where -- you know, where there's no actual killing going on or about to go on or a high risk of such violence, then you are absolutely free to say anything you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's have a break. We'll have a longer break than usual, at the request of the interpreters, and we will resume at five after 1.00 and we will continue until 2.30, 2.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing will resume, and I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it's good now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you gave me a pretty satisfactory answer to my last question; namely, for -- for speech to be legally punishable, it has to be made directly in a spot, in an area that make it a risk, a possibility of crime, when it -- where it can lead to crime. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is -- is that what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I just summarised in two or three words what you explained at great length, so I would have to be in an area, in a locality where combat is going on, and then my speech would have to incite somebody to commit a crime. That is the gist of what you said. I cannot tell you verbatim. My question was: When in the American legal system - I'm simplifying my question now - when would speech be punishable as such?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If you forgot what you said, let's move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I think this is asking for a legal question and Dr. Oberschall's expertise is as a political sociologist, and I think this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he cannot give a legal answer, he'll say "I don't know." If he has some knowledge on legal matters, he can say "maybe I can answer." It's up to you. Mr. Seselj asked a question. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to say that here this -- this is -- we're talking about a specific jurisdiction here and not other jurisdictions and not international law. We're not dealing with international law here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert and I'm not here to testify on such fine legal distinctions. And I -- I merely said what an ordinary citizen following, you know, current events and debates on these questions would -- would tell you, but I'm not a legal expert, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, I'm asking you about your knowledge. You are a professor at an American university and you should be a very educated man and very familiar with public affairs. The last thing you said goes to incitement of crime. You don't have to know the legal definition, but I am summarising what you said, which you perhaps forgot. However, I have new questions for you. Please listen to me carefully now. Let us distinguish between events in the Serbian Krajina, in Croatia, and events in Serbia and in events in Bosnia and separate them from the events in Hrtkovci, Vojvodina, et cetera. So let's look at these two things separately. There's one war between the Serbian Krajina and Croatia. Another thing is the war between the Republika Srpska and the Bosnian federation, and the events in Serbia and Vojvodina are yet a third thing. Now I'm asking you only about events in the Serbian Krajina, in Croatia, and the Republika Srpska and in the Bosnian war. I'm asking you: Did you anywhere in my speeches, in my articles, anywhere, in any public appearance, find a passage where I advocate killing prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, killing prisoners of war, you don't advocate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I at any time in my speeches advocate killing civilians?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, you say things like "amputate" and "blood will flow," and you use this kind of language. A lot of people, including myself, interpret that as violent actions against a -- an entire group of people. In this case, you know, Croats, or whoever -- whatever the context was. So I -- I didn't say it was an illegal speech or I didn't say you didn't have a right to say those things. What I coded that kind of thing is "advocates and expects violence," and that's what I was asked to do, to content analyse your speech, not to pass on the legality of it or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're evading the answer. There is legally authorised violence and unauthorised violence, and from my speech about rivers of blood, you can conclude that I, as a person, am bloodthirsty, but that I talk about rivers of blood does not mean that I am inciting anyone to kill civilians. Am I clear now? This is not a legal issue. This is an issue of social and political psychology.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you say "rivers of blood will flow," I -- I don't interpret it as slaughtering pigs and -- and goats. I mean, I think you're referring to human beings. So I'm -- that's -- that's my interpretation. You're not talking about animals that are going to be eaten and butchered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you do not know Serbian literature and Serb heroic epics that are full of passages about blood flowing, but it's about blood flowing in war. Two armies clash on the battlefield and blood flows in rivers. We have a whole cycle of these Serb popular epics that talk about that. It's one thing to talk about blood flowing in rivers, and it's another thing to say, "Go on. Kill Bosnian or Croat civilians." Whose blood is it about? The blood of soldiers in the battlefield. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you say. But if you look at, actually, the military events, both in the Croatian and the Bosnian war, most of the blood that was flowing was not that of soldiers but of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And would you agree that blood of civilians flowed in rivers on both sides?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it flowed on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, did you find any excerpt from any text where I would be advocating the killing of women and children or inciting anyone to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't say it in so many words. I don't recall any passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Oberschall, you, as an intellectual, should know that there is a great number of judgements of the Supreme Court of the United States clearly defining what kind of instigation or incitement has to exist to make an act punishable criminally. It has to be direct and immediate. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said to you and the Court that I'm not a legal expert. If -- if you want to have testimony about the -- the -- you know, the constitutional history of how these legal terms are defined in the case law, you should get a -- a lawyer here to testify whose expertise it is. It's not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Oberschall. When you were doing your expertise, you did not put into your computer programme, into your search engine, attitude toward civilian, attitude to prisoners of war, attitude to the women and children of the opposing side; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All we did put into the search engine was "Serb," "Croat," "Muslim," "Albanian," in the -- in the right languages. That's what we searched for. Passages that deal with Serb/non-Serb political relations. We didn't search for anything else, the weather, women, old people, tariffs, agriculture, nothing like that. Just -- just those top -- just those key words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Oberschall. I asked you this to let everyone know that you did not get hold of a single statement of mine where I advocate honouring international humanitarian law, humane treatment of civilians, women, children, and elderly of the other side, et cetera. Mr. Oberschall, in your searches of my texts, did you find anywhere a passage where I would advocate, incite, or instigate to unlawful detention? So I'm talking necessarily about civilians. Only they can be unlawfully detained.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean taking hostages?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Taking hostages as well, unlawful arrests, or any other way. Any other way that can be used to unlawfully detain civilians, that is, without a court decision.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall -- I don't recall any such passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't recall because it doesn't exist. Did you find anywhere in my texts a passage where I advocated, incited, or instigated torture, any form of torture?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Torture? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oberschall. Did you find anywhere in my texts a passage where I advocated, incited others, or instigated cruel treatment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you mean by "cruel treatment." We had a long session last -- yesterday, actually, on expulsion and exchange and ethnic cleansing of -- of populations, and, you know, your advocacy, your views on that point. And I would say that's cruel treatment of people not in the sense of a narrow definition of "torture" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, we had agreed at the beginning of this session to distinguish everything that happened in Vojvodina from what happened in the Serbian Krajina, Croatia, Republika Srpska, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember? So this exchange of population that relates to Vojvodina, let's leave it aside completely for now. We'll come to that later. Let me tell you, for instance, what cruel treatment is. Rape is cruel treatment. For example, because there is no precise definition of rape in the international law of warfare, it comes under the category of "cruel treatment." So did you encounter anywhere any advocacy on my part, incitement, or instigation to cruel treatment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like rape?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Like rape, let's say, or any other form.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did -- no. You did not advocate rape, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you find anywhere, with the exception of Vojvodina, any appearance or text of mine where I advocated that anybody should be departed from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Republika Srpska, of Croats, of Muslims, anyone? Did you find anything like that? Forget for a moment Vojvodina and Kosovo. I just need you to --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I forget Kosovo? I mean, that's part of Serbia and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times you advocated -- you practically advocated that everyone who's an Albanian should somehow get out of there and go back to Albania or some other refugee camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- run by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, wait till I get indicted for Albanians or something. Albanians are for the time being not in my indictment. I haven't been charged with that yet. I'm asking you specific questions, and I want a specific answer. Did you find it anywhere that I advocated deportation of Croats from Serbian Krajina or deportation of Muslims and Croats from Republika Srpska? Here. It's a specific question.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really have to look through the records that I -- that I coded, some 30-and-some records to see exactly what you said at the particular dates that you were active in the -- in the Krajina. I can't produce it from memory, but we have the quotes in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But in your expert report, there is no mention of that. There is no quotation. It seems I've read your report more carefully than you did. I claim that there is no mention of that, and you find it now in the expert report where it is, but please don't take too much of my time leafing through. You don't know of a single such example. And that's a statement I'm going to make. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Seselj is mischaracterising the testimony, and he's asked --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- Dr. Oberschall to look in his report to find an accurate answer to the question, and I request that he be given the opportunity to do that. Perhaps if Mr. Seselj wants to concede that the information is there and that the report speaks for itself, we can conserve time, but the witness should be given the chance to get the accurate information that he has in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go briefly over this. This is the problem. The accused Seselj is asking you whether in his speeches or in his texts he mentioned at any time deportation. That is the question. It's very simple and straightforward. So deportation either of Croats or Muslims. So in your report, was this noted that at one point in time, on such a day, in such a speech the -- there is mention of deportation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's many mentions of deportations, and I quote from some of these texts. Right now from memory, I can't sort out whether they referred to Croats or Serbs in particular parts of the Krajina or -- or Vojvodina, but, you know, if the Court wants me to provide this evidence, I can sit down tonight and read through the records and -- and give you a full documentation and give the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have the report and we can do the same exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I absolutely don't care what Mr. Oberschall is going to say tomorrow. I know for a fact that there is no example whatsoever of my advocacy of deportations, speaking of Muslims and Croats from Croatia, or Republika Srpska, that is, from the Serbian Krajina in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Oberschall, did you find it anywhere in my texts that I advocated forced transfer of population within the Serbian Krajina or within Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Krajina itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. "Forced transfer" means within the borders of one state, because "deportation" means transfer from one state to another state, to explain to you the finer legal points.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I mean, we -- I found in the content analysis a lot of mentions of deportations. I would have to look at the specific quotes and dates to -- to identify those that refer to what Dr. Seselj just referred to as "deportations within the Krajina." I -- offhand I can't-- it would take -- it would take a lot of time to go through this now record by record, and I'm quite willing to submit in writing after looking at it, after the conclusion of this session, to give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, at least in my trial you will never again have the opportunity to make any written submissions. You've already made all you are ever going to make. You have already had several years to prepare for this trial, and now I'm finding out before this Trial Chamber whether you prepared well or not. When the water goes under the bridge, it never flows back in that same water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection. This is not a question. It is a lecture to Mr. Oberschall about whether or not to answer the question in writing that he's been put to in the courtroom. It's improper cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, did you anywhere in my texts related to the same areas, Serbian Krajina, Croatia, and Republika Srpska and Bosnia, any examples where I would advocate, incite, or instigate to wanton destruction of villages in populated areas and devastation that is not justified by military need? Did you find anything of the kind anywhere, from what you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't really know quite what you mean by "not justified by military -- by military need." I mean, that's a very loose term. But I would say in general, no, you didn't -- you know, you didn't do a sort of a Genghis Khan act and say we have to destroy everybody and kill everybody and rape everybody and so on. You didn't do that, no. In the text that I looked at, you didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oberschall, and thank you for having been concise. Mr. Oberschall, in my texts, in my public speeches, in my written texts, anywhere, did you find me instigating, inciting destroying religious buildings or educational institutions; that is to say, churches, mosques, schools, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any in my content analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oberschall.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other things, though, that were quite objectionable, but they refer mostly to the Albanians in Kosovo. But do we go into that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Leave Albanians aside. Never mind the Albanians. Now, we are going to have big flows of blood, rivers of blood on account of Albanians. If they take Kosovo away from us now, blood is going to flow in streams, for hundreds of centuries --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is absolutely improper. This is improper for Mr. Seselj to make threats of violence against Albanians in connection with the current political question being debated in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor says that you are making threats. What can you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I am reacting to the witness bringing up the question of Kosovo yet again. I cautioned him several times that Kosovo is not part of my indictment, and my questions have nothing to do with Kosovo whatsoever. How can I stop his speech about Kosovo when he is wasting my precious time? Stop, Mr. Oberschall, don't refer to Kosovo any more. When they indict me for Kosovo in some other trial, then you can talk about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Oberschall, the accused is not charged in the indictment with issues related to Kosovo; therefore, any mention, unless he wants to put questions regarding Kosovo to you -- but if that is not the case, do not mention that topic. Let us remain focused on the report. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, in excerpts from my speeches, did you find me anywhere advocating the plunder of public or private property or me instigating others to carry out that robbery?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in your -- in your -- some of your statements, you certainly describe and refer to a lot of plundering and robbery of private and public property that was going on during ethnic cleansing in Bosnia. You, of course, always say, when you describe these events, that Milosevic and the army and the Defence Ministry forces and the special forces were doing it but your volunteers were not doing it and that you were telling them not to do it. Frankly, should we believe that? I mean, that's what you're saying. Was it true? But it's -- but that's what you were saying. And then that is in the statements that I content analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you're not expected to believe or disbelieve something here. You're just supposed to confirm or challenge some factual allegations. Now you've moved a step ahead.
