You establish that I criticised others for having plundered private or public property, and you do not have a shred of evidence of me advocating that plunder. Am I right? Am I interpreting your words right now?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you were accusing others, a lot of others, doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste any more time on that issue. Mr. Oberschall, in the excerpts from my speeches, did you find any case when I advocated the commission of inhumane acts in the territory of Republika Srpska or the Republika Srpska Krajina? Any kind of inhuman acts.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't. You didn't. There is no such thing. That's why you --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, let me -- can I say something? Again, I mean, I would have to go through those specific statements about ethnic cleansing and figure out in terms of the date and their location whether or not they refer to Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. I'm not -- I can't on the top of my head answer that question without referring back into my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're an expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, in this regard. Since the accused puts question as to what he may have said in his speeches and writings, with regard to the crimes referred to in the Statute, I was looking at your method of analysis, and I wondered about this, why did you not add some columns that would be more specific? For instance, deportation, change of population, shift of population, rape, murder, cruel treatment, and then you could have ticked where appropriate. Did you not think of that sort of methodology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had a way of cross-examining the -- the group and what was happening to it. For instance, ethnic cleansing, referring to these various people. And had I known that I would be cross-examined on it -- I didn't think it was important as to which group in a particular group was being referred to by Dr. Seselj. But had I known that, I could have used our software to do that analysis. It's just that I didn't know I was expected to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Chamber's edification, there are 415 records, and I, as part of our legal analysis, have superimposed on that the elements in the indictment, and I can provide that kind of graphic analysis with the counts in the indictment and the relevance of the individual records to that. I considered that would be part of our submissions in summation of the evidence that we've led and how it relates to the charges in the indictment. If that would assist the Chamber in determining the admissibility of the records analysed by Dr. Oberschall and his report, I'd be happy to submit that to you now, as opposed to later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, I raised the question with the expert, and he answered it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, counsel for the Prosecution cannot now add on something to what the expert is saying. When I re-examine Ms. Dahl, then she can say what she has to say. This will never be the case in this particular case - maybe in some other proceedings - because I have charged her. But now I am asking this witness -- this expert witness questions, and he is supposed to go on talking about this, because he dealt with my case for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In my texts, Mr. Oberschall, did you find any reference to my advocating in the territory of Republika Srpska or the Republika Srpska Krajina any kind of persecution on ethnic, racial, or religious grounds? What does persecution mean? Layoffs on account of the fact that somebody is a Muslim or a Catholic, or somebody being forbidden to buy certain supplies in a store because they belong to a certain ethnic group or religious group. Any kind of persecution, that is to say, discrimination. If somebody is an inhabitant of Republika Srpska or Republika Srpska Krajina and if they belong to a different ethnic group, if that person differs ethnically from Serbs, did I advocate discrimination against such persons? Have you come across any such thing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean things like employment discrimination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Employment too, yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- well, we weren't looking for that, but I wasn't -- I didn't see in your texts anything about employment discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oberschall. This concludes the set of questions that I had with -- that have to do with Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. Now we are moving on to what happened in Vojvodina. Mr. Oberschall, you deal with a great many excerpts from my speeches where I advocate deportation of Croats from Vojvodina, exchanges of population, exchanges of property, and so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is a considerable number of such examples. And I am not denying that. That is true. Did you notice -- did you notice that all these examples date back to a period that involves three or four months in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they all date to -- to that particular period. I'd have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You are not able to answer this question. Mr. Oberschall, you say in several places that I say that Tudjman expelled 200 or 300 thousand Serbs from Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. Whether it's true or not, it's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did not even try to establish whether that was true or not; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have -- well, these -- the numbers have -- have really not been established by -- by an authoritative source. I -- I would think that this Tribunal in some of its prosecutions would end up coming up with probably the best numbers that -- that we can have. The way you use numbers in other contexts leads me to be very skeptical about the numbers. But I don't think the numbers here really matter that much. We can divide them by 10; we can divide them by 5; maybe we can even multiply them by 2. I mean, there's terrible injustices being committed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, don't give answers to questions I've never put to you. You could have gotten the figures from the statistics office. There are lists of refugees that were revised several times. You didn't ask for any of that. Have you heard of Professor Svetozar Livada?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is a professor of the University of Zagreb who published a few study papers on the expulsion of the Serb population from Croatia. You should have consulted him. The Prosecution has used his analyses. Let me tell you one more thing. No one was tried before this Court for the expulsion of Serbs from Croatia in 1991 and 1992, and I am being tried because only a few thousand Croats left and none of them were expelled. Mr. Oberschall, do you know that in Serbia at the end of May 1992 there were elections that were held? This is 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to believe that they were not held, if you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But you don't have any knowledge of them being held either; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I want to check on Serb elections, I go to sources like Goati and I find out who ran against whom, what the political parties were. This is not something I carry in my head all the time. Why should I?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, these were very important elections. These were the first elections for the Parliament of the Federal Republic of the -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia after it was constituted in the spring of 1992. You would have to know that as an expert for that period of my activity. You appear here as an expert witness and you don't know about these elections.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I don't know about the elections. There were elections going on all the time, many different elections. If I want to find out something about a specific elections, I know the source to turn to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, that is not an answer to my question. You had very narrow excerpts of my speeches made available to you. To be aware of the broader political context in which I speak, you would have to look that, in terms of Croats in Vojvodina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I read up, actually, on what was happening in -- in Vojvodina and throughout the period 1991 to 1993. I read a number of things both on the military and on the political front, both in Bosnia and in Serbia. Yes, I -- I looked at that material very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Oberschall. You mentioned during the course of the examination-in-chief my speech from Hrtkovci on the 6th of May, 1992. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, if it's in the -- if it's in the records and the examples that I content analysed, then they're there. In your speeches there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course it's there. Of course it's there. On what occasion did I make that speech?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what speech you're referring to. I mean, can we go to a particular record or an example where -- that we're discussing? I mean, you're asking me how --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, this is my renowned speech, the one I made on the 6th of May, 1992 in Hrtkovci, and this entire section of the indictment for Vojvodina is based on that. That is the key speech, the fundamental speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Dr. Oberschall asked for a record reference in order to be able to discuss a particular aspect of his report, and I'd like to ask the accused to please give Dr. Oberschall the record reference so that we can hone in on his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. You're referring to a key question, that speech of the 6th of May, 1992. In the expert's report, on -- in which page are we going to find this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This morning, during the examination-in-chief, from 9.00 until 10.30. What page? Believe me, I don't want to look up the page. There is no reason for me to do that. That is the key speech that the indictment is based on. I'm now going to ask Mr. Oberschall about what it is that he concluded about my speech. I just want to check whether he read that speech of mine in its entirety. It is contained somewhere else too, but that I'm going to tell him later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you're asking about my content analysis of your speech, you're referring to a particular statement. I content analyzed something like 400 records. I don't know them by heart. If you tell me where this statement that you made or statements that you made from that speech are and how I coded them, I would be glad to do it by referring to it. It's not fresh in my memory. I can't do that just without seeing the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understand you properly, at this juncture, when Mr. Seselj talks about the 6th of May, 1992 speech in Hrtkovci, this doesn't cause any immediate reaction. Is that right? Because you mix it up or it is mixed in the 400 other documents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- it's in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge. At that point in time, I could not think of such a clever question. With that question of yours, you replaced the ten questions I want to deal with after that. Yes, this does show the competence of the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecution has my entire speech, Mr. Oberschall. And this speech was publicised in several times; the last time in my book "The devil's advocate, the criminal Pope of Rome, John Paul II." So if you had looked for it, you would have found it. You could not have written your expert report without having the text of all the speeches of the rally in Hrtkovci. Right? Because that was the key rally for the indictment.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you give me the speech and give me a little time, I'll content analyse the whole thing for you right now. I don't have any problem doing that, as long as it's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not giving you the tiniest bit of time. Not a bit of time, Mr. Oberschall, because practically you had to know that speech of mine by heart as an expert who came to testify here about my advocacy in favour of Croats being deported from Vojvodina. I'm not giving you a single bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is not cross-examination, Your Honour. This is arguing with the witness. We didn't ask Dr. Oberschall to focus his analysis on the indictment or to cherry-pick the speeches to try to help us prove the case. We gave him 44 volumes of material and he made a search for key words and phrases and analysed those parts of the speech, in terms of propaganda, threat discourse, sending threat messages, and all of the themes that we've talked about for two days. But this is not proper cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very proper cross-examination, but Ms. Dahl hasn't managed to learn that yet. I'm going to teach her, and soon at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, the speech made in Hrtkovci was a pre-election speech, and from the content you could have --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting to the discourse in the courtroom between -- Mr. Seselj should not direct his comments to me directly. He should not threaten me. He should not indicate what lessons he wants to teach me. It is going to be a very long trial if I am going to be made to be battered by his discourse here. This is cross-examination of a witness, not attacking the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, refrain from addressing or challenging Ms. Dahl. You may think that the Prosecution did not do their work properly or not thoroughly enough, but do not attack her personally. It is not necessary. As if she would attack you -- if she were to do so, I would say exactly the same. . Let us continue, though, because this is an important topic. Please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, first of all, I issued no threats to the Prosecutor. It was just a promise, rather, because from my way of cross-examining witnesses during the following months and years, she will learn a great deal. That is my profound belief. And I have the right to say that after the many inappropriate interventions she made here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, therefore, you do not know that I made a pre-election speech in Hrtkovci in May 1992. You did not know about that; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it was a pre-election speech, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You didn't know that because you did not have the text of the entire speech; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I only had the -- the experts that our search produced, which dealt with relations between Serbs and -- and non-Serbs. At that time, in that particular place I thought that that was probably the most important part of that. That's what we picked up and analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Oberschall, you are quite right, but I am saying that your methodology was not appropriate. Did you notice, on the basis of these speeches of mine that you analysed, or parts of these speeches that you analysed, that in all of these speeches I either set out a programme as to what we radicals are going to do once we come to power after the elections or I call upon the existing authorities to do that, to carry out an exchange of population, to deport Croats, to apply the principle of retorsion, and so on and so forth? On the basis of these excerpts, could you gain knowledge to the effect that all of my speeches are either a promise as to what we are going to do once we come to power or a request for the current authorities to do the right thing, to make it possible for Serbs to move into Croat houses, to apply the principle of retorsion, and so on and so forth? Could you come to that conclusion on the basis of these fragments?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I'm supposed to conclude. Yes, you -- you talked about all those topics that you mention, and some of the statements that I content analysed do cover all those topics, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not only topics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj. Let me react to your answer and to the question, which is at the very heart of the matter. When somebody makes a speech, that person is either in a position of being a decision-maker or is a potential candidate in order to become a decision-maker. If we are talking about a pre-election speech, you have candidates who are not going to be decision-makers and those who are in power who make the decisions. Would you make a distinction as to the contents of speeches, depending on the precise situation the speaker finds himself in, between the fact of being a decision-maker or a potential candidate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, if you are in a position of authority, then you can -- you can implement some of the -- some of the programme or policies that you advocate. If you're not in a position of authority, you -- you can't immediately do the same thing, because you don't have the authority. As I see it, Dr. Seselj, when he was a candidate for various offices, was already a member of the legislature. He was the head of an important political party that was at times in coalition with the existing Milosevic government. So he was in a position of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. In order to gain time, if you are a member of the legislature, you can be a decision-maker. But if you are in a minority party, you are not a decision-maker, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but you can be in a coalition that is part of the governing coalition, or that goes along, or that, you know, has cabinet posts in a coalition. So, yes, all these things are important, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, it is correct that during the second period I was in a coalition with Milosevic's Socialist party of Serbia, but do you know from when until when?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you. From the 24th of March, 1998 to October 2000. Did you know that before?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I claim and state that that is the only period where I entered into a coalition with Milosevic's party. And we have no -- and you have no proof to prove otherwise. You just haven't got any evidence to prove otherwise. At the time, I was the vice-president of the government of Serbia, the vice premier.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already had this morning a number of statements which I refer to in my expert report that during a much earlier time than March 1998, you had really privileged access to the Serb television, state television and media, and that was part of a political deal between you and Milosevic. Now, you can say you might not have had a formal position with a title in -- in the government, but we're talking here about political alliances and -- and political coalitions, and that gives you power, sometimes even more power than if you're a minister or vice-president, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of what research, Mr. Oberschall, did you arrive at the knowledge that in 1992 I had a privileged position in the regime media? What research was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was research -- you know, you say 1992. This was research done in Belgrade by people who did media research of all media, TV, magazines, newspaper, radio, and so on. And I could actually, from this research, in my expert report -- there's actually several pieces of research that were done on the -- on the Serb media, and -- and your access to them. So that's in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why are you thinking up all these things for 1992, the research for 1992? Why are you inventing all that when it's quite obvious that you have absolutely no idea of any research of any kind? Why are you inventing that, and there's none of that in your report either.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you're saying. But if you read my report, you will see it. It's all in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All there is is your assertion that I was privileged and nothing else. There's nothing else written down like that. Mr. Oberschall, do you know that in 1992 in Belgrade a book was published, "The screening of the elections," and the authors of that book are two women, Milivojevic and Matic are their surnames. Mrs. Milivojevic is now a professor of political science at the Belgrade University and it was the magazine Vreme that published the book. And it was financed by Soros, the US Intelligence Agency, other Western services and foundations. Have you ever heard of that book, "The screening of the elections," "Ekranizacija Izbora"? You don't? Fine.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't read things about alleged secret plots and, you know, paranoic kinds of reports about what happens in politics and in back rooms and so on. I go by evidence. And there's a lot of stuff that I just can't get into, because it's -- it's really not -- it's not really factual. It's just imaginative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall -- Mr. Oberschall, if you had a keener intelligence, you would know that --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I here am not mentioning foreign services. There's no grounds for objection here, no grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: There's no grounds to insult the witness. This is improper cross-examination. And I ask that you curtail the examination, because it is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please do not tell the witness that he is more intelligent, or this or that. We are not here to say anything about intelligence, neither you or I or anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I here before you and your colleagues only mention research on the representation of political parties and the presidential candidates in the media dating back to 1992, which was conducted in Serbia, and in order to show just how unbiased those results were, I am giving the background information, who printed the book, who financed it, and so on and so forth. So I am moving to the advantage -- I am speaking in favour of the unbiasness of those facts, because it was the opposite side, the enemy side that printed it, so it doesn't matter whether I'm right when I speak about the CIA, Soros, or whatever, although I am right in what I say about them. But the important thing is that the book is unbiased, it is not prejudiced, and it shows that the Serbian Radical Party and I, personally, were least represented in the media compared to all the other parties and sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this -- I'm not criticising the question, but if this book, the reference of which you gave us - and it's probably an interesting book - but if this book was not read by the witness, that has nothing to do with the intelligence of the witness, of course. Witness, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm embarrassed to say, but I have to take a two-minute break in the toilet, if -- if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's take a five-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, please may I remain in the courtroom? Because I can't keep carting my things off and bringing them back if it's just for five minutes. May I be allowed to stay in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, and we'll come -- we'll wait here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] -- to contest the quality of the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters were not listening because we thought it was a break. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying the following: Mr. Seselj, you're entitled to proceed with your cross-examination, ask questions, and provide the Trial Chamber with all elements so that it can make a decision as to the expert quality of the witness or not, but you cannot assess or draw any conclusive assessment as to the quality. This is up to the Judges to do this. And you cannot either make any direct assessment of the personality of the witness. Do not do this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Lattanzi, I understand you completely, but allow me not to accept what you've just told me. And I would like you to look at practice, the Anglo-Saxon practice of cross-examination, especially the examination in the Oscar Wilde trial and also practice in cross-examination conducted by Prosecutor Geoffrey Nice in the Milosevic trial. I am far more lenient, Mrs. Lattanzi, far more lean and mild. And I find this witness so likable that I am extremely mild towards him, and I promise you that I'll be much sharper to other witnesses. That's my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must try to be moderate at all times. Let's resume, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, that's not in my nature to be moderate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, you mentioned the force of my political party, the Serbian Radical Party --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I need to -- to interject about what Mr. Seselj's nature, his natural tendencies has to do with his ability to represent himself. And if he is unable to effectively comport himself in compliance with decorum, respect, and dignity towards witnesses, if he is unable to restrain what he calls his "nature," then he needs a lawyer to be appointed to represent him, because he cannot use his right of self-representation and his nature to abuse witnesses, to abuse this Court, to abuse me. His cross-examination must be incisive, careful, and appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, follow the rules. You cannot abuse witnesses. Witnesses are trying to answer your questions. Of course you have the right to challenge their credibility and test their credibility, but do not make any personal judgements. This is not appropriate. You told us that maybe it's your nature to get into that. Well, refrain yourself from it. This is in the interest of all and in your own interest. Substance is of the essence and substance only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, if I consider that the witness is lying, then I have every right in the middle of this courtroom to say so, to tell him he's lying during the cross-examination. So please do not restrict my rights. Several times here I have found that the witness was lying, and you are witnesses to that, and so with interventions like this, Mrs. Dahl is actually trying to turn this trial into a circus. She doesn't like my cross-examination, the way I do it. Well, I prepared it in the way that I knew she would not like to begin with, so you can caution her not to make inappropriate remarks and the threats, to take away my right to defend myself? That's ludicrous. Who can do that? Who can curtail that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, my fellow Judge told you earlier that you are entitled to many rights in cross-examination. You are entitled to ask questions, but you just said something extremely serious. You're saying the witness is lying. The witness is under oath. Lying is a serious offence when you're under oath. So you can't just say that outright if you cannot demonstrate it and prove it. Otherwise, you could just say that everyone's lying. Let me remind you that contempt of court -- perjury, you know, is something that could lead to seven years in gaol. So be very careful with what you're saying. Sometimes I think you're going -- saying things that go beyond what you're thinking, when you're saying that the witness is lying, well, he might be lying, but prove it. Just don't say it outright. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I wanted to echo what you just said. The credibility determinations are reserved for this Trial Chamber, and the personal opinions of the accused are not appropriately expressed towards the witness in the courtroom, proper cross-examination should be designed to indicate whether there is bias, mistake, or malice, but hurling invectives at the witness or calling him a liar is not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you want to demonstrate that the witness is lying or making errors, do this, but do not fly off the handle. And demonstrate what you are trying to say and demonstrate your theory. And if you cannot demonstrate and prove what you are putting forth through your questions, then we're losing -- we're losing -- we don't know where we're going any more. And just before this incident, we were dealing with a problem of substance. And I would much rather spend time on substance than waste time on anything -- of course, you are right to try and demonstrate that the witness is lying, but be scientific in your demonstration. It's not because the witness has not read a book that he's lying. Maybe he just didn't read this book because he thought the book was of no interest, which doesn't mean he's lying, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the witness here said in front of you that it was on the basis of some sort of research in Belgrade that he established that in 1992 I had a privileged position in -- by the ruling regime media, and that kind of research just doesn't exist. So how, then, can you qualify the witness other than the way I did? Tell me, please -- that means I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard what was said regarding research done in Belgrade in 1992, on the role he played in the media. So was there research; yes or no? Could you please give us some enlightenment on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was research. I have an entire section of my expert report on the Serb media, on the Serb media's role in the -- in the elections in the early 1990s. And I cite, you know, several sources on this. And it's just a matter of turning to those pages. You want me to do it? I can read it. But you can read it. He can read it. Everybody can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that there was research done. Let's continue now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I state that the only research was the research I mentioned for 1992. Now the witness says there was. I don't see it. Mr. Oberschall, you mentioned here that my political party had a significant role in the political life of the country at the time I held the speech -- gave the speech in Hrtkovci. Right. Now, how do you measure the importance of a party in a country's political life?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wasn't asked to measure the importance of any political party. That wasn't really part of what I was doing here. I was analysing your political discourse and evaluating or coding it on these kinds of themes and techniques of propaganda. I'm not -- I'm not here to testify about the political parties and coalitions in -- in any kind of a detailed fashion. It wasn't part of my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But why are you then saying that my party and I had a significant role in political life if you didn't measure that as -- as a sociologist by empirical measurement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually indicated in the section on elections and so on, as to the number of votes that you got and that other people got in certain -- in certain elections, and that certainly is one way of measuring political influence. But that wasn't part of the central part of my assignment. You know, if you want more detail on that, it's -- it's all documented. It's available in Goati's book on -- on Serb elections in the 1990s. And I quoted from it to -- to make certain points, but it wasn't part of my overall analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, we're talking about the rally of the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci and what I said there on the 6th of May, 1992. Now, do you know how many deputies the Serb Parliament has, how many members of parliament?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll tell you straight away. 250. And do you know on the 6th of May, 1992, at the time of the rally in Hrtkovci, how many members my party had in the Serb Parliament, how many deputies?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you're an expert, Mr. Oberschall. Try and remember. Think about it. I have to insist.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, Dr. Seselj - and this has come up again and again - that you think an expert has to have, you know, an encyclopaedic mind filled with a lot of facts, and if he can spew forth statistics, that makes him an expert. My view, and that of many other people, is that what an expert is is somebody who's knowledgeable in a certain area, who's worked in a certain area. And if you want detailed factual knowledge on a certain topic, the expert knows where to get it and he gets it and he uses it appropriately. And that's what I'm here for, and that's my role. I'm not an encyclopedia. If you -- if you want to know all those details, you know, go to Google or consult some -- some big encyclopaedic source. I'm not an encyclopedia. I'm an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Oberschall, I'm an encyclopedia, a universal encyclopedia, law, politics, sociology, physics, chemistry, mathematics, psychology, even biology. I know it all. What I can do? I know it all. Mr. Oberschall, as an expert you said that my political party --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no sense in this, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be interrupted all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can only raise an objection when I get the interpretation. It is not proper cross-examination to boast about one's professed fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said this already. Mr. Seselj, you were talking about the 250 members of parliament and you were asking the witness how many members of parliament were in the SRS, came from SRS. It might be interesting for the Judges to know. So just tell him: If I told you that there were so many -- that's how you should ask the question. Otherwise, I'll never know the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one person, I myself, nobody else from the Serbian Radical Party was in the Serbian parliament, just me. And there were 250 seats. Now, an expert who doesn't know how many deputies we had claims that we were highly influential in the country's political life. That makes no sense at all. So that's why I asked my question, Judge, and that's why I continue to challenge the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, let's now move on to your main report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving to the report, Mr. Seselj just said one thing. He said that he was alone in Parliament. So being alone in Parliament, does that have any consequences as to the power he may have in terms of decision-making? If you had known that, would you have -- could this have changed anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that it's really true. I mean, it's hard for me to believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the assumption that it would be true. Maybe he's lying. But I don't see why he would lie here, to the Bench. So start from the assumption that he was alone in Parliament at the time. What conclusions can you draw from this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- the conclusion I draw is contingent. If -- if -- if he's elected just from one constituency, I don't know, in Belgrade or someplace with 20.000 votes going to the Radical Party and he's a deputy, that's one thing. And -- you know, in 250 seats for the whole of -- for the whole of Serbia, then that would not make him an important political actor. But as far as I can tell, the Serb Radical Party, his party, got several hundred thousand votes in -- in all of these elections. I know that somewhat later he got -- he and his party got about a million votes out of something like 3 or 4 million. So whether or not you are alone as to represent your party if you've got 20 -- 20 per cent of the total country's vote, it makes you an important political actor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall, in any research in the field of social sciences, whether histriography, sociology, and even psychology, especially social psychology, and so on and so forth, it is important to have certain time coordinates. Isn't that right? Now, I'm asking you what the force of my political party was on the 6th of May, 1992. And you are telling me what happened in the coming years, in the years to follow, how many votes we had. In 1992, May, we just had one deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection. Compound question. Mr. Seselj needs to ask one question at a time and allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please try to ask short questions with -- that require short answers. Otherwise, if it's a compound question, we're going to get lost.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, my question is a very simple one. I am warning the witness. I am telling him to look at the time span that he's talking about, the 6th of May, 1992, the Serbian Radical Party had just one deputy in the Parliament of Serbia. In December 1992, it had 73. But that was seven months later. So I'm talking about the time in which I advocated the deportation of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You state that we were a serious political factor in the political life of Serbia, and I'm challenging that, and you don't have a single argument to back up your assertions. Isn't that right? You don't even know that we just had one deputy in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is a speech followed by, I'm not sure what, Your Honour, but it's not proper cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, your question is too long. The question is a speech. Let me tell you how the question should have been put to the witness. This is what you should have asked the witness: During the May election the SRS had one deputy. At the next election in December the SRS obtained 73 seats. So now that you are making a judgement on the power of the SRS, were you able to make a difference between May and December? And if you had made a distinction between what was the case in May and what was the case in December, would that have changed anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a tremendous change, from 1 to 73. I mean, it's -- that's a tremendous change in -- in terms of a 250-seat Parliament. And, let me see, the ... And yes, I was not aware of the fact that on the 6th of May, 1992 the Serb Radical Party had just one deputy, Dr. Seselj. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, allow me. Just a small correction. I was elected at the additional elections into the Serbian Parliament in June 1991, and until December 1992, I was the only MP from my party to the Parliament of Serbia. However, in May 1992 the elections were not into the Serbian Parliament; they were into the Federal Parliament. I believe that this precision is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So at the time of the speech in Hrtkovci on which this entire segment of the indictment is grounded, we had no more support than that. Mr. Oberschall, you said you studied the events in Vojvodina. I suppose you know the events in that territory well. Give me a direct answer to this question: Were there any attacks on Croat civilian population in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were. The -- there was a report by Tadeusz Mazowiecki who was working for the United Nations -- United Nations agency looking at human rights and -- and other violations in -- in all of the former Yugoslavia, and several of those reports refer to what was happening in the Vojvodina just about at this time, and there -- there are many examples there of -- of people threatened, of people fleeing for their own safety, of -- you know, and other violations of human rights, and that's -- that's all been very well documented. So I -- yes, that's what I've looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Oberschall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we have to finish for the day. It is indeed 2.30. The interpreters seem to have problems. We shall resume tomorrow at 9.00 for you to complete the examination-in-chief. You have used so far 2 hours and 35 or 40 minutes. I don't know exactly now, but I'll tell you tomorrow first thing in the morning. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 9.00. The sitting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.33 p.m.,
